-Hut now it's—good-bye. hiss me, mcaara, my lover, my own." "Bless you, my blessed.* He was standing by her and caught her again, and kissed, her passionately. "Yes, it's good-bye." "Fether," she called, and George Gretton came out. "I'll go," she said, with trembling lips. "Good-bye, sir." "Take care of yourself," said Gretton, with shamefaced friendliness in his eyes. Awl Richard nodded. Gretton shook hands, and, turning, left left the room. "Oh, I can't, I can't," cried Madge, desperately. , But Richard caught her up:.

"My wife to be, good-bye." He put her out of the door and shut it upon her and leant against the wall for one dizzy moment. Then, as his brain cleared, he ran to the window, and, opening it, leant out and saw her look up. And then the desert opened for him, and in it were Honour, and Disaster, and Glory, and the struggle of man against man and against the elements.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Royalty at the Ward Wedding.—The Queen put off, for the first time, her mourning for her father, the late King of Denmark, at the wedding of Lady iNfary Acheson, and Mr. Robert Ward, and appeared in a very beautiful gown of mauve crepe de chine, with a toque to match. The Princess of Wales wore a pale blue and white muslin dress, much trimmed with lace, and a tasselled rope of seed pearls encircled her neck. Her Royal Highness appeared to be in the best of health and spirits, and it was remarked how much slighter she has become since her visit to India. Royal Toilettes.—lt has long been noticeable that the Princess of Wales is as faithful to blue as Queen Alexandra is to mauve. It is rarely indeed that he Royal Highness appears in a toilette untouched with blue, in some shape or form, and this colour suits, the Princess to perfection. Another item in connection with the always perfect dressing of the Princess of Wales is her disapproval of the elbow sleeve for out of door wear. Her Royal Highness has all outdoor toilettes built with sleeves that reach the wrist, and with these the Princess wears the short three or four button gloves. Signs of Early Antumn.—The approval of autumn is apparent in the milliner's showrooms, where the speckled feather.' of the pheasant, and the wings and quills gathered from the farmyard are finding a foremost place. Unhappily, birds are all too likely to be seen again later, upon modish "creations." and apparently nothing can be said to induce some women to forego this particularly heartless and altoeether objectionable mode. Brown fiats and T-lair.—For several seasons past, the all-black hat has found a place in the fashionable woman's wardrobe but its place has been usurped this summer by the all-brown hat or toque, for which there is quite a craze. Milliners are also tilting much of their headgear by means of great choux of brown tulle or chiffon, and it is no uncommon thing to see divan' colored hats raised at the hack or side in this way. The idea appears to be the blendine of hat and hair together into one harmonious whole," brownhair, of a medium shade being, by the way, the choice of moment, the dying of hair goes steadily on increasing, hut women are showing greater sense in canoeing more natural colors, and therefore the process is less easily detected. White Mourning.—A famous London modiste is doing her best to persuade her customers to mourn in white —pure white dresses, and toques, with long white veils thrown back, and falling well below the waist—but the fashion is not likely to become popular. The few with leanings towards exclusiveness in dress, may and doubt- less will, take the idea up, but the many will certainly remain faithful to the sombre crepe gown and veil, familiar to us as a garb of woe. Bargains in Furs.—July and August are the best months in the year for the purchase of furs, in September prices rise again therefore the bargain hunter has little time to lose. White furs are greatly reduced at the moment, and this state of affairs is no doubt due to the rumour that white peltry will be out of favour during the coming irinter. Dark furs promise to reign supreme, an item of news which will be wel- come to the imnecnnion' s as they are so much more economical than the white varieties. Moreover dark furs are sea rule, snore becoming than white ones. Modes for the little ones.—Many mothers are die- pensing altogether with petticoats for their small girls during the holiday season, and the notion is an excel- lent one. Knickerbockers made of the same fabric as the dress, take their place, and the child is much more free, than when cumbered with underskirts. Shady hats too, have greatly taken the place of caps, which is another change for the better. The craze for sandals again, has almost worn itself out, and thin openwork socks or stocking, and loose comfortable shoes are being generally preferred. Fashions in Complexions.—A colour, real or " applied," has long been deemed a necessity by the Society woman, but we have changed all that, and now a colour is not correct. Instead. a complexion of ivory, dusted with pearl powder, is the one most cultivated. The disaapearance of the rouge pot, is of course a move in the right direction, still it is to be hoped that np-to-date women will not fly to the opposite extreme, and go about looking like ghosts. A really healthy complexion snd,colnue.are the (Ines to be desired and sought after, and the wise will leave rouge and powders severely alone. Gas-Cookers.—Hitherto it has been mostly the rule of the great monopolist corporations to act on the oppo- site to the principle that their interests and those of the public are identical. Many of the railway companies for instance still appear to believe that people must travel, and must therefore be made to pay as much as possible for the privileee, and offered a minimum of facilities and conveniences. Many of the gas com- panies, however, are now adopting a more enlightened policy, and one of the greatest of these concerns in London is offering to send out, free of charge, lady instructors to show how the best result may he obtained from gas-cookers with a minimum consumption of gas. There is a double objection to waste, for apart from the expense, if the gas passes off unburnt, it is unhealthy and lends colour to the objections which are often urged against gas cooking by people who regard it as a sort of slow poisoning. Properly managed. there is nothing harmful to food in gas-cooking, and it is one of the most economical methods, if care is taken to avoid the necessity for unduly turning up the gas for want of time, and leaving it on after it is required. The Care of the Teeth.—The teeth should always he well brushed at least twice a day—in the morning, and before retiring at night—and a medium and not a bard brush should be used. Farther, the inner side of the teeth should receive as much attention as the onter.and the month should he well rinsed afterwards. In be matter of tooth powders, precipitated chalk, used in conjunction with good soap will keep the teeth per- fectly white and clean. This should be used in the morning only, once a day being sufficient in which to clean the teeth with powder. Any extreme of heat or cold is exceedingly bad for sensitive teeth so also are acids, while minerals containing iron should always be taken through a straw.
MADGE.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Wycliffe Congregational Church.

Owing to the closing of the church the services in connection with the above body are being held in the Co-operative Ball, Sankey-street. The first services were held there on Sunday when the preacher both morning and evening was the Rev. J. Yonge, whose addresses were listened to by largelcongregat)ions. Free Church Open-Air Campaign.

The open-air campaign under the auspices of the Warrington Free Church Council, is being conducted with great enthusiasm. On Sunday, meetings were held at Catherine-street, Bridge Foot, Penketh and Latch- ford, and were attended by large crowds. The services are attracting increasing attention and there is every prospect of their object being attained.

div.head: Buckley-street Church.
div.p: Buckley-street Church.

Camp meetings in connection with the Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street were held on Sunday. In the morning, a large congregation in Cobden-street was addressed by "Happy Jack," the converted collier; Tom Bold and Mr. Dews. Several solos were well rendered by Mr. H. Woolley. A large number of people assembled in Catherine-street in the afternoon, and in the Church in the evening to listen to further addresses by the same speakers as in the morning.

div.head: Presentations to Catholic Priests.
div.p: Presentations to Catholic Priests.

On Sunday evening a general meeting of the congre- gation of St. Mary's, Latchford, was held in the school- room to receive the report of the Presentation Committee. Father Roache presided over a large attendance, and was supported by Father Marrs. It was decided to present Father McGrath with a purse con- taining £5O as a token of esteem and respect and in appreciation of the great amount of work he has done for the mission, and also to show their sympathy in his present ill-health. Father D'Arcy, who has lately been transferred to Altrincham, and has for the past four years so ably assisted Father McGrath, will be the recipient of a suitable memento. A vote of thanks to father Roach° for presiding was passed.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

There were good congregations at the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday. In the morning the Rev. A. C. Parker preached his farewell sermon, basing his remarks on Rev. xix. 4. The preacher in the evening was the Rev. S. Pitt who gave an interesting account of the Wesleyan Conference at Nottingham, at which he was present. He dealt chiefly with the great enthu- siasm and liberality shown when missionary matters came np for discussion. The debt of £lO,OOO had, he explained, been wiped off and two gentlemen had each promised annual subscriptions of £3OO, whilst others had promised sums ranging from 000 to £loo.—During I the service the anthem Hark, hark, my soul," was I ably rendered by the choir.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

An open meeting of this society was held in Winwick- street Co-operative Hall, when in consequence of the very fine day, there was only a fair attendance. Coun- T. Burton presided, and said when he bad attended those meetings he was struck with the large number of young wen present. lie felt they could not be in a tetter phle aud advised them to make their acquaint- ance with older men, with sound experience, and try to emulate them in all that was good and noble. The old generally looked backward to their experiences ; the ' middle aged were sometimes too busy to look either Ibackward or even forward,because of the great pressure of business, but tried to do their duty for the time being, but the young they lived for the future, making their plans, and placing their ideals before them. A wise look forward, and a very careful choice, of roads • that led to success, was very commendable. Mr. Tom Harrison the converted carter of Oldham, gave some very humorous tales of his past and present experience. His address was earnest upon the evils of drinking, smoking, swearing, and gambling. Mr. Pearce presided at the organ. Mr. Joseph Hawthorn, and Mr. A. Healey also took part in the meeting. Mr. J. W. Willett sang in his able style "The Sailor's Grave" and "Calvary." The contribution to the organ fund was £1 10s. Bd. A collection was also taken.

div.head: EDUCATION IN AGRICULTURE.
div.p: EDUCATION IN AGRICULTURE.

EXAMINATIONS OF THE ADVANCED DAIRY AND POULTRY STUDENTS AT THE COUNTY COUNCIL FARM. The Examinations under the Lancashire Education Committee were held on the 17th, 18th, 19th and 20th of July, the examiner of the Dairy Students being Mr. W. J. Grant, Director of Agricultural Education for Monmouthshire, while the Poultry Students were examined by Mr. F. W. Parton, Instructor in poultry- keeping at the University, Leeds. Mr. Grant reports as follows : PRACTICAL WORK :—" This has been well and thoroughly taught; those who received instruction fully appreciated the fact that every detail, no matter how trivial, should be well and carefully done, whether in the manufacture of cheese, making of butter, or Icleaning the dairy and its utensils ; smartness with a splendid thoroughness gave plain evidence of the every- day routine at your excellent Farm School." LF.CTURES AND CLASS WORK :—" I was very much struck with the aclmirhble manner in which the majority of the students whom I examined not only understood the best methods of modern dairy work, but also the manner in which they had so thoroughly grasped and understood the principles that underlie everything they had been so well taught to do, a fact that speaks for itself as to the excellence of the instruction given. Mr. Parton reports as follows :—" I am pleased to report that the work done by most of the students is very excellent indeed, both practical and theoretical." , The Lancashire County Council offers free education to farmers' sons and daughters and others engaged or likely to be engaged in Agricultural pnrsnits who are residents of the administrative county of Lancaster,and in addition makes an allowance in aid of board and lodgings in Preston, or for travelling expenses thereto. The classes are held at the Harris institute, Preston, and the session lasts from about the last week in Sep- tember to the end of April in each year. Education, with board and lodging, is given in butter-making and cheese-making, milk sterilization, bread-making and poultry-keeping, free of cost, to students attending the dairy school, at the County Council Farm, Hatton, near Preston. Instruction in butter-making and cheese- ranking is given where required in the county free of 035 t. Lectures and advice are given in agriculture, horticulture, beekeeping, and poultry-keeping. Valu- ahle scholarships and exhibitions are offered annually. Further particulars may be obtained from the Director of Education, County Offices, Preston.

div.head: DRESS-FASH lON-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASH lON-HOME.
THE HOLIDAY WARDROBE.

The blouse is the backbone of the wardrobe during the holidays. So many different sorts of blouses can be worn with one skirt that it saves almost half the space that would be taken up by whole dresses. The skirt of a light afternoon gown will be quite suitable, says a fashion writer for wear with a dinner or theatre blouse. Another space-saving garment is a long coat of white or pale blue alpaca. This can be used as a dust-cloak, a garden-party wrap, a shower-coat, or an evening coat for casino wear. Unlined clothes are AO much smaller in compass than lined, that it will be found advisable to take as many thin blouses as possible, with a couple of under-slips, and perhaps a very light woollen Spencer for the colder days. If it is necessary to take an evening dress, there is nothing like black. It does not crush, and it is suitable for a larger number of occasions than anything else. It is a very good idea to take off any such loose trimmings as fichus or falls of lace, and to feld them separately. They do not take long to sew on again, and this makes all the difference in their condition. It is always a nuisance travel- ling with a lot of luggage, and for the majority among us who go without maids it is a perfect nightmare.

The automobile is changing everything in France. It has powdered the hedgerows I..nci forests with white dust, it has Awakened the od. villages. it ha.s changed even marrialms. •in t.,41 good old days, when • there 'was no "tcuf-teuf " vibrating beneath my lady's bower, when Romeo had to scale the wall with a rape, and employ ether primitive means to deliver the lady Irc:n her father's castle, an elopement was a clifEeult and dangerous operation. Now it has become as easy as the smoke of petrol (and of grease.) The motor waits beneath the. garden wall. Tim gate opens, revealing a vista-ct rose-trees and a maiden fair. Quick! there is no time for poetry. Manly arms encircle the feminine waist, and the dainty burden is hoisted into the car. Romeo is disguised in great goggles and a chauffeur's coat of loather... The engine throbs—so do their 'hearts. A touch of the lever—away! away! Papa pursues; a huge outcry. Ffteen days pass, rapturous days. Married in distant town; re- ceive tardy blessing of parents, who recognise game is up. And this, declares the Sketch, is how they elope in France. It is quite the fejnion. THE ETHICS OF CROQUET. • .ht

1 Croquet has been rightly termed an immoral game, says Lady Phyllis in the Bystander. I ; don't meaii to imply that it cannot be tremen- dously interesting, but it tires people out with a weary, not a healthy, fatigue, ruins the temper, and certainly encourages its advocates to be ' spiteful. Even the sk i ill s directed more to the deliberate discomfiture of somebody else than in any other kind of game. Then, again, it is such a cool and collected thwarting of the enemy's plans, and loses all the brilliance and energy of the more rapid description of sport. It reminds ono of a sulky, premeditated attack of temper, in comparison to a mere hasty word.

div.p: A SON OF EMPIRE.
BY MORLEY ROBERTS, Author of "The Western Avernus," "Strong Meg and True," "The Earth Mother," "Red Earth," "The Great Jester," &c.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIII.
So she kissed him on both cheeks. "I've had a ,big row with mother to-day," she remarked a few minutes later.

'So I guessed at dinner." "And I told her I wouldn't marry Bobby, and that I'd never marry anyone but—Richard." Mr. Gretton jumped as if he had been shot, but Madge held him. "But it was only on general principles, so o speak, dad; and, of course, I never told her any- thing else. And she was most trying. Oh, why did she get him out into the Soudan? " Mr. Gretton moved uneasily on his chair. "I feel I ought to tell her something about this, Madge." It was Madge's turn to look startled. "Oh, you forget I told you in confidence. , "But she is your mother, Madge." _1 "I can't help it," said Madge, firmly. But whether she could not help holding hrm to his word, or help Mrs. Gretton being her mother, she did not say. tell her myself when the time comes, she declared, viciously. "And I shall like doing it. And I'll keep you out of it. And, dad, to- morrow is to-morrow." She sighed and softened for to-morrow was to be good-bye to Richard. "I'm so unhappy," she murmured; and presently she was sobbing, and a vast sense of desolation overwhelmed her. "Good-night, dear father," she said, suddenly, and kissing him she left tears upon his face. "Ah, I've lost her," said, Gretton, "and when she goes-" Yes, when she went the world wourd seem a very wilderness. He felt resentment against Riehard Blundell rise in him once more. And yet this was destiny. She might at least be happy and have no unloving thought of her solitary father; for now George Gretton knew that he was solitary and that life, save for,his children, had been a failure. He did not regret deceiving his wife; she had been no helpmate to him. But as he passed Madge's door he stayed and leant against the wall. She was thinking of . her lover, not (it him. If some day her father was to be only a memory to her, that memory should at any rate be without any thought of bitterness. He felt strangely old and broken, and when he went to his own room he lay awake till long past mid- night.. But his child dreamt of vast plains under the relentless tropics, and as she sought for her lost lover she watered with tears the thirsty sand which had drunk the blood of many heroes. So the night passed for her and for her lover. And when the cold clear dawn of early winter walked in thin hoar frost, Richard was up to finish his work, before her footsteps ,faltered upon his stair. And this hour was his hour of bitterness and revolt • for, mistaking his real strength for weakness, he wondered how it came that he should have been weak enough to accept the task offered him. What advantage paid for the incredible toils of the desert, what honour renewed a man's wasted trength ? To work for the Empire seemed in the hour of dawn and disillusion striving to augment the vtl/41t proportions of a devouring polyp. It was a unit wasting itself for many millions ; it was adding one to infinity. Chronos and Empire both devoured their.childran. And yet to plant the flag of Britain in 'dark places, to drive out the slave-raider, to bring order into chaos,' to say "peace" where there had been no peace, was, after all, something, were it not that he now suspected he was not only a plaything of Destiny but a pawn in the hand of his enemies. He felt, he almost knew, that this gift of command was a gift of the Greeks. Turner was moved by Fielding, Fielding by Madge's mother. The thought took- the honour out of his work; he was a mere slave. _ _

And yet again, for Madge's dear sake, and for the sake of confounding alien machinations, he would make it honourable, make it successful, make it even glorious, if only half the strength of , his youth remained to him. If he gave up Madge , and the delight of her love for the time being, he I would bring her back a crown. And then she came in with her father. She found him in another room, which he had taken I specially for this last day. It was indeed two rooms, for a curtain divided it. She knew why he had done it, and her father knew as he smiled a little sadly. "So we've come," said Gretton. And Richard held both Madge's hands. "You are very .kind, sir. I leave to-night for Brindisi." He felt Madge shake, but she looked up at him bravely. Why would her lower lip tremble so? She bit it hard and pressed his bands tightly. "When shall we see you again?" Richard looked at her through a thin mist. , "In less than a year--with luck. And now my luck has turned, owing to you, dear." She came closer to him, and Richard put his arm about her. Together they faced Gretton and , a sharp pang of pain struck through him. Though she returned home again for a year, yet she had really left him for ever. • "Oh, say good-bye," the father cried, with odd impatience, and a ring of anger in his voice. He turned away, and found Madge clinging to him. "You don't love me best, now," he said, in a choked voice. "Isn't it—different?" asked Madge, whispering. ' "0 dad, dad!" He caught her in his arms and kissed her fore- head, and with a twisted smile looked across her bowed head at Richard. _ - -

-„.._ "Here, you pirate," he cried, soft and fiercely. "Say good-bye to her and don't come back for years." Richard took her. "Months if I can make it. I'm your son, sir. Bless- you for her." The curtains fell behind George Gretton. He 'roped into a big chair and looked at a book down. Oh, biat the world was upside down! But for them it was a material world, a world of pain and joy incredible; anguish crowned itself with roses and joy wore cypress. "I have so much to say to you," she cried against his heart. -"Say it." "I can say nothing—nothing." "My dear little girl." He knew she could say nothing. In such an hour speech fails. At the height of all thought, and passion, and emotion is silence. Upon the mountain peak no rain falls ; in the loftier air a storm is silent as th 3 grave. "Come back to me, come back to me!" She looked at him dry-eyed, and on her cheeks was a ring of fire. Cry, Madge." "No, I can't, Richard. I've a year for that, :a year. She moaned a little on his shoulder_ "I don't understand." • He did not ask her what. "But I love you, love you, Madge." She closed her eyes. "I know it. Come back to me!" He took her in his arms and sat down with her. "You are strong, are you not, Richard?" "Oh, Madge, I'm as weak as water—to you." .:Bat to others ?" tie kissed her lips and strokpd her hair. "There are no others." "And never were?" "And never were." She knew he did not speak the truth, but s}. e loved him so.• "Would this have been worse if we—had bee I Tarried, Richard?" She felt him tremble. "I lli ink much worse, Madge ; and better too.' "Come back, come back !" He held her to his heart and stared at the wall for a long, long inintite. "I'm not brave, Richard, I thought I was." "You are brave, my darling, but—" "But what ?" "This almost makes a coward of me." She rose.and looked him in the eyes. "Oh, no, you cannot tell me that. I'll be wilt you every hour, every minute till you come back." Ile kissed her again. "And then you will be with me every hour every minute for ever." " Ves."
- i
She looked him in the eyes again, and COlow poured into her face, and again the flood receded, and left her very pale. But she rose up.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIV.

So the world wagged and went its way, and peace was in every border of the Empire for the space of a week or so. But the pot that boils never ceases to simmer on the British fire, and in Burmah (where poor Captain Melville did such great things, not here related) Dacoity flourished at times, and in Gulistan, where swords were beaten into plough- shares for a moment, there was growling; and in the Niger there was a brew on hand, and on the side of Nyassa another kettle of broth, and down in the Transvaal much pitch hot, and in the Soudan hell to pay, and in Egypt talk of Khartoum, and in Abyssinia blue blazes, and in the background of it all England, and France, and Russia, and Italy, and hateful Germany. In the midst of the Africa medley, walking discreetly in a den of lions, went Blundell, and at home Madge watched him as some may have watched the ancient prophet, or as the bystanders looked on the fiery furnace seven times heated where Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were reported to have received no scathe. But Richard of the lion-heart, new Cur de Lion, dropped from her view and was lost in haze and hot sunsets, and never a word was spoken, though it was told casually in a paragraph that he had gone hunting in the back of Somaliland. But those who hunt lions bring back treaties, and the papers were discreet—or, without information. Even Madge got but one letter from Zeila and another from near Harrer, and then lost him. He 'said he could write no more with any certainty of her getting it. But, above all things, he impressed her to believe nothing she heard about any disaster occurring to him. For it is the way of news that a very black devil kills a fairer devil from a mountain and says ifts has slain an accursed half-caste. And those who hear it say he has killed a Portuguese; and by- and-bye behold it is ,a white man. Then the cut- up stranger is called an Englishman, or a French- man, or a German, or an Italian, and four families are on the stretch. Then News, alias Rumour names him Captain This or Viscount That, and Baron The-other, and there is weeping over an alien and forlorn carcase now fleshless to the hungriest vulture. So he warned her ere he was swallowed up. And at first she was comforted. But imagination grew like a gourd; and the sense of pain, 'after the stun of his going, was again upon her. She went like a young widow, and wore her darkest dresses and hocl her storms; for in her desert stalked the Red Simoon of her mother, and Madge buried her head in her cloak and waited till the whirlwind was overppst, and roe up pale and choked, but utterly determined. As one month crawled by, a long, glow, thirty- jointed reptile, another came, and she had no comfort. Companionship was alien. Annette was rejected like dry bread; the sole gift of the gods to desolation was her father. . She clung to hica pitifully, and he brought her carefully selected books of African travellers who returned; for she devoured those with fear and trembling which told of them that came back no more. One gleam of light came and one only. When at last the list of Gulistan honours came out Richard was among those who were henceforth entitled to the letters D. 5.0. Old Briggs had the K.C.S.I.' and little Gwynne the V.C. "Richard ought to have had that, too," said Madge, but she was almost content. The political situation of the House of Gretton was sadly strained as the days passed, for her mother had really believed that the departure of the intruder would bring peace where there was no peace. But this ferocious commandant of the home could not even proclaim "That order reigns at Warsaw." For rebellion stubbornly visible in hostile ayes• is not true order. She began to ! perceive dimly that things had gone far beyond her largest and most ungenerous suspicions. For now she lost her ally; Bobby Maitland said in I painful and almost disrespectful slang that it was "no go," and sullenly refused to continue a court- ship which he saw was hopeless. He was, at any rate, a gentleman, and he recognised that Madge found his attentions positively distasteful. She t was no longer rude to him. That was a bad sign. That she never smiled and treated him as an amiable automaton, wound up by her mother, dis- gusted him entirely. He refused to be wound up any more. "I tell you it's that Blundell," said Bobby. "If she forgets him or if he's killed I'll C. about it." He retired/on Pytchley in fair order, and Mrs. Gretton avenged herself on George. "George, you are encouraging, her," cried Amelia. "I have long suspected it. You bring her books about Africa." George found himself muttering something about "geography," but her eyes appalled him. About. Afrira ! Where that man, whom I will not mention, has gone." George remembered "she had lunch with a man on a mountain," and he almost smiled. With 'care he turned the smile into a ghastly contortion and postponed the Deluge: But, all the same, he felt disloyal to this icy wife of his. "Well, my dear, what's the good of tryire, to snake Madge what she isn't? You may take a horse to the water—" • "Don't answer me with vulgar proverbs. I will net be answered with vulgar proverbs," cried Amelia. , "And you evade a plain question. You are encouragin her to disobey me.' It was so abssolutely true that George wriggled like a fish on the ~,rains. But he picked up some' courage and replied, with a rebellious look which was marvellously like Madge's best: - "I want my daughter to be my friend." Amelia looked at him through her glasses. "You acknowledge it?" George frowned. "Confound it, Amelia, don't look at me like that !" She looked at him more like that than ever and
George jumped up. "She shall marry whom she likes. There now!: I'll not have her bullied." He rushed into his own room and slammed the _

door and Tleft Amelia 'like a grounded iceberg. After sonic ten Minutes he got afloat. • "She shall not marry whom she likes !" And she sent for her doctor. With his aid she reduced George to a fair show of penitence ; .for this is one of the chief uses of a physician. But he would not entirely retract what he had said. He apologised for the slath, but would go no further. He pointed out that Madge would very soon be twenty-one, and that with her Character opposhion would be fatal. Amelia was put to an extremity. "You know she would not outrage society by marrying against our united wishes." "H'in," said George, uneasily. "I'm not so sure of that."

Ile certainly was not sure of it in one sense, for if she married Blundell she would not do it against their united wishes. And now he was Richard's advocate. lle•had gone over utterly to the enemy. 'They were again in the country, and Christmas and the New Year had passed, leaving devastation in their wake. But fortunately it was an open w:nter, and George got plenty of huntinv.. To his sturlse Madge would not hunt. He extracted the reason from her with the utmost difficulty. " Well, then, dad,- I'm afraid." "You afraid?"
He spoke with the intensest surprise. "I might break my neck," said Mad;e, nervously, "and• Richard- "Wouldn't, like it ?"

"I was thinking' I shouldn't like it," stid Madge. "It would be so foolish to do it—now." Sie dipped into the future and was lost to him. ITernther sighed. "A 1 don't you ride too hard," slie said, waking up ; "Fin nervous about you, too." She could not face the remaining months alone. "I understand," said George Gretten, sadly, and vet with a smile.
"What should Ido without you " cried Madge, with a selfish shudder.

So she walked alone in the park and stood by the lake a lonely and pathetic figure. Water attracted her terribly. She was always thinking that perhap, gichard wanted some. And hero it lay, cool and deep and dark. She sat down on a fallen tree and picked up 1 handful of sand at the edge of a rabbit burrow. A handful of sand! An acre of it! A million, million, tons of it spread out burning under a burning and most awful sun. And in her mind she SW the map so familiar to her. Here Was fertile Egypt and the ancient Nile; there the broad Soudan. Khartoum, and Berber, and Kassala far, far away. Then Abyssinia with its barren fastnesses, and Darfour and Kordofan. It opened out and grew. She saw the waste spread beyond mental vision; not an oasis in it. But on it was the sound of camel bells, and Richard went alone, or 'Richard was fighting, or Richard lay dead. She saw his bones and shuddered.

So it was in the day, and at night the Devil was fantastic and more populous, being peopled with creatures of drowsy imagination. Little devil folks, dwarfs with poisoned arrows, incredible giants, gigantic blacks, the Arabian Nights, they all waltzed on sand blown by simoons. And as she suffered, even as she imagined thirst, he might be dead of it. She went without water for a long day, even fee two. She drank in a' fever,. but conunit ted that folly no more, for it fed her imagination too dreadfully. He might be calling to her now, even now. Never a night passed but she rose up when she heard- him. And she was helpless and could not go. So she dreamt, and sometbnes Heaven sent her a good dream, and she marched and fought with him through whole worlds of famous adventure, and was his happy, happy helpmate. , The months drifted and the winter passed, and she was pale. She never mentioned Africa save to her father, and now she spoke of it to him very seldom. The papers said nothing of Richard. And spring came, and again early sumer:far. She started to think that it was two whole ystirs since she had met him at Chilloa. Two years, were so little and so much. She was a woman now. It was a century ago, oh, more than a century. They were in London once more, and her mother whimpered through the old dreary social round. They went out to dinners ; tl.e'y went to "At Homes," and gave receptions. Mrs. Gretton ate sweet things, and was ill. The doctors came and put her on a diet to save her from herself. She got better and shewed herself. She dragged Madge with her, and abused her for lack of interest in the" gay world. , "Don't look like a ghost!" "I am a ghost," said Madge. But she never spoke to her intimately. They had no more real quarrels. Her mother almost feared her.

Even a London season passes. So this one passed like the rhododendron flowers in the Row. And still Africa was silent, and no letter came from Richard. They went back to Gretton Park, and stayed there during August and September. She walked among the autumn leaves, and saw the Desert, the grim unanswering plains of Death. Was she dying too? She felt like it at times ; for her joy of life gave' way utterly in the • hungry suspense of that unceasing year, and her heart went with no delightful rhythm., She faced the prospect of life without him, and a cold hatred of her mother filled her to the white lips. Then she weakened, wept, grew easier, and hoped. But Mrs. Gretton found her child's eye upon her with inscrutable passions in it, and a subtle vision for defects in that noble character. The ferocious egotist quailed on the dissecting table; she grew nervously conscious of defects, and hardened her heart as she broke down under the microscope. Madge's scalpel' touched quick nerves and the patient-winced. She ate less, and denied herself, and was more than ever a victim; more than ever a vampire. She was friendless; for she could admit no one to her mind; she entertained acquaintances on her mental doorstep of painted marble leading to stucco. Her manners in public were perfect, and of the latest fashion. Manner, in the singular, she had none. She wanted her way, and, being heartless, got jt for the most part, and at the end of her journey-found no one there. She marched like the Plague, and was received like it with whitewash and disinfectants. But in her arid mind she perceived neglect, contumely, insult, and never suspected that she sowed the crops herself.

And now she felt that her husband was on the verge of revolt against usurpation. To lose her sceptre and tinsel crown was to be finally rejected of Life. She perceived no refuge after that but the Church: no mitigation, but good cooking and a mild curate. In truth, she was going through the bitterest tragedy, of woman's life: she was fifty, and had earned no compensations: had laid up no treasure, that moth could not corrupt, in the heaven of home. Jealousy of her beautiful daughter touched her sharply at odd seasons, and at the lay- ing on of powder. How dare the girl presume to demand and to command an empire that her mother could never have aspired to? The child would be rich, was beautiful—she had been neither. And the mother was not loved, and sometimes hungered for mere affection without having the grace to obtain it. Like other tyrants she fell back on tyranny, and was obstinate on an insecure throne. The very resemblance of rule would go if this man returned from tip desert. She dared to pray for his death, and faced her daughter with half a sneer and that satisfied acquiescence in the will of Heaven with which folks of grace perceive ill winds that blow them good. That Make grew pale and less abundant in vitality was not unpleasing to her. But as the girl grew pallid she grew aloof and dignified. Some- times a look which was half-pity drove her mother frantic, and in such a mood she was almost ready to let the alien take away the rebel. But, again and again her overgrown and monstrous pride in domination came to help her. She thrust it between father and daughter, and chased George Gretton into his den: he got no peace over a pipe, even though he smoked hard to drive this bee out of his last retreat. He resorted to nerve shattering measures, and took to p. brand of tobacco that half choked him, when she buzzed in upon his solitude. Then disaster fell on her: she had her weapim, or her chief weapon, snatched from her. She had grown to put much trust in the knowledge of Madge's great crime, and kept it for the private battlp. She dropped dark hints about it to her husband, and for a time he said nothing. But in a moment of irritation he quite forgot Madge had asked him not to speak about it,

"What do you mean ? " he asked, testily. Mrs. Gretton shook her head. "You do not know your own daughter." "I do," he answered', visibly annoyed. But Amelia thought she knew better, and said so With much bitterness.
"If you mean about the telegram, I do know," cried aretton, puffing cough compelling clouds, and Amelia collapsed like a pricked bubble. "She has told you ? " "Yes."
"And you—oh, good Heavens! You do not mind?" "What's it matter ?"

This was so incredible a thing that for once Amelia had nothing to say. She did not even snort as she conveyed herself from the room with all possible speed, and sat in her own boudoir to consider how she had built and on what insecure foundations. She had been living in a kind of fool's paradise its far as this fact was concerned. Like an ancient philosopher of the pnrely deductive type she had dwelt in the region of hypotheses, squaring her facts to her theory. And now her theory was a rickety toy. She smelt defeat and wm humiliated. Madge and her husband were alike hostile, deceitful. But worse than all she had never given either of them credit for it. And they must be definitely banded together against her. But even now, with her small brain, she never imagined it possible that the subdued George, so long ago defeated and taken captive, could be Madge's confidant and ally to the very uttermost. This passion of the girl's seemed almost shameful since it was against her inother's wish. If it was shameful the girl must know it, and could never speak of it. So ran her logic. But Heaven above witnessed, so she assertect.that her child's best interests were her own heart's desire, and while she livet+ Mae should not have her way. She feigned more friendliness, and sometimes, when she imairined that Blundell might really be dead, she was almost friendly. And then Madge's closed , heart opened a little ; she believed she must be to blame in some measure for the strained relations of the house.

Another summer passed, and again it was autumn, and a cold autumn in the country. The leaves fell earlyi but an early frost came, and renewed itself thrbugh the last months of the year. ' The hunting was uncertain, and George's temper was uncertain too. He had little comfort in his life, and at times he eyed the wife of his bosom with positive distaste. And then was a whisper, as of tragedy. hinfloo erl.lll 11 rlWT,s,hrPairrn-qt lanouid and Dale.
t3he looked for the paper and did not see it in its usual ,place. Her father seemed uneasy and alarmed ; her mother's cheek-bones were flushed.
----- "Where's the paper ?" "There," said her mother, pointing to where It 46tburnt part ofr it over the fire—accidentally,"i said her father.

But his voice, was unsteady. Madge started and looked at him. She took up the paper and found a great piece of the burnt page missing. She stared at them both, and then pushed her chair back from the table. "Why—did you burn it?" : "Eat your breakfast," said her mother. "No," said Madge. "Father, what was it that you did not want me to see?" She was as white as a ghost, but her voice was quiet and firm. "Nothing," said her mother. "What was it, father?" "0 Madge!' ' "Was it about—Africa r • She whispered it, and lo iced at 'per mother as if she were some far-off forgotten thinz. And her father did not answer. His jaw dropped and his lips quivered. "It was about Africa," cried Madge. "Oh, you shouldn't have burnt it. For I trusted you!" "What did that mean ? " asked her mother. "Tell me what it was !" And her father told her while his wife sat silent. "They say he's killed. Oh, it's not true," said Madge. "I know it isn't true. I just know it." She turned to her mother and eyed her silently for a strainPd minute.

"But you believe it, and are glad. I'll never forgive you, mother." And she left the room. Her father followed her, but she shook her head when he spoke in the hall. "It's not true," she said, wanly; "go back to her and tell her I'm engaged to him. Oh, she's a cruel woman!"

Twenty minutes later she rode past the breakfast- room window on her way to Gretton to get another paper, and George turned to Amelia. "This is your -doing." "What is my doing ? " "If it's true it will kill her." "You want her to marry this beggar ? " "If she likes, woman," said George, sternly, and Amelia fell back in her chair. "I believe she'd be ham. " "She said she trusted you. mean ?" she asked, fiercely. '"hat she said, by 4eaven "cried George pas- sionately. "Oh, did you ever have any heart She can trust me."
What did - she.

He flung out of the room in an agony of pity for his daughter, and left his wife staring out upon the grey morning. It was an hour till Madge returned, and she came in to find her mother still sitting over the dry and chill remainder of her breakfast.

"I've read it," said Madge, "and I don't believe- it. Richard told me not to believe anything that, was said." "He told you ? " cried his mother. "Yes, he told me before you and Sir Dan sent him away to kill him." Her mother rose up, and stammered incoherently. "Look at my hand. that's his ring," said Madge, in strange triumph, "and if he does not come back I'll wear it till I die. You sent him away ! " "I did not."

"Yon did. I know it. Oh, why could you not hare a spark of pity? Did you ever love anyone, anyone ? " "He's dead," cried her mother, "and I am sorry." In that moment she; was almost sorry. "He's alive, and coming home to me," cried Madge. "But if he was dead you would be glad. What i he to you that you should *ant him dead? I'm not a child now. I'm myself, my own, and his Oh, do you hear me!" Her cheeks blazed in circles set in ivory; her eyes, dark-ringed, burnt into her mother's soul. "Oh, you know nothing!" cried Madge. "Oh, poor woman, I pity you 1"- "Go !" said her mother, choking. "Go!" And Madge went.to her own room, and sat for a long, long hour over the news which she did nbt believe. She never shed a tear. And when she came down to dinner that night she discarded all things mournful, and shone in scarlet and gold and wore a red dower in her hair and one upon her heart.

SMALL HOLDINGS MOVEMENT.

Lord Willoughby de Eresby, M.P., is disposing of a considerable acreage of his property in Mid-Lincoln- shire in order to give a practical stimulus to the small holdings movement. Three out of a series of sales have just taken place, and nearly all the land has been sold. At a sale at Old Leake the average price obtained was £7O an acre. At Stickforci the sale realised £7,367, and at Vainfleet atd Burgh £23,000 was obtained for the property sold.

div.head: AUGUST BANK HOLIDAY.
div.p: AUGUST BANK HOLIDAY.

Many of our renders will be looking forward to .spending a shortenor longer holiday in the Emerald Isle, and to such we would point out the exceedingly low fares hy the Tedcastle Line,as advertised in another column. This year, their fact steamer " Blackrock " has been arranged to leave South side Nelson Dock at 8.30 p.m. on Friday. 3rd August, returning from Dublin at 4 p.m. on Bank Holiday. Should visitors wish to prolong their stay in Ireland, the tickets as far as the trip to •Ind from Dublin is concerned—are good for two months, without extra payment. The S.S. " Cumbria " will also be despatched on Saturday at 10 p.m. for Whitehaven, and the English Lake District, proceeding from Maryport to Dublin on the Tuesday, and leaving 'there on Friday at 2.30 p.m. due here again in the small hours of Saturday morning The tickets are available for 2 months, to return from Dublin by any later Ted. castle steamer.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 4, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 4, 1906.

, dencect lucky fellow to have won her anections. She was unhappy with her first hueband, you know —an old brute of seventy ill-natured years of %elf- (ndulgent age. But you're not marrying Pot-belly as well "—I looked up ang:lly at the epithet, ana he smiled—"well, the Baron Grostof ; and, look here, don't pick me up and break me in twc pieces or snap my neck if I remind you that he's a Russian, and a wily one, and has always had t, peculiarly warm welcome, either at his hotel or at that charming Cannes villa of Madame's, for an 3 and all Englishmen who have the good fortune tc be Queen's messengers." "I really wish—" I began warmly, but he got, up and out me short. "Don't bother. I must say ta-ta—have to go": and he sauntered off, turning at the door to grin good-naturedly and yet warningly. It would be absnrd to say that his words had no effect upon me, because when Baron Grostof came up on the terrace that evening and was most effusive in his congratulations upon the news which his niece had given him of our engagement I found myself looking at him most suspiciously, and seeing double meanings in all he said, and trying to imagine what a eletective would do whe "...nted to trap him. But my suspicions fled fast ...zough when Mignon came, for the Baron went, tbrld we passed a delicious hour in that dreamy, balmy air, which is fittest of all atmospheres for a love scene.

That evening and the two following days fled like a dream, and it seemed but a couple of hours before Mignon and I were bemoaning together the hardship of the separation that the morrow would lriag with it. "You will hukry out again, Hugo ?" she said, wistfully, "The 'hours of your absence will be leaden-winged." . "I can only go where the Foreign Office bids me, Mignon," I answered. ruefully. 'I may get out here again soon; I hope so. 'But---" I shrugged my shoulders and tried to smile. "And do you carry despatches to-morrow?" she asked, with her innocent, wistful smile. "Hateful despatches, that part us." - "Yes; that's what I live to do? " "What a dreadful life!" she cried, in a solemn voice. "Always carrying secrets—and I suppose you mustn't look at them. I couldn't resist." "Oh, yes, you could, child—if it was your duty. They are nothing to me." "I should\die of curiosity," she said, large-eyed in assumed wretchedness. ' "Curiosity can't fight against one's sense of honour, my dear. I—but never mind about that. "4./11 me, what are your plans? How are you going At help our meeting'again ? " - At that a singular change came over her. She seemed to cringe and tremble, and her eyes looked frightened. "I have a presentiment—it must be a presenti- ment. lam afraid of your leaving me. Oh, I wish I could tell you! " i "Wish you could tell me what, child?" I asked. , "No, no, no, no, no," she cried, repotting the, word vehemently many times and shaking her head.l 'I cannot! The Baron--" "It is very late, Mignon. I have been looking for you," said the suave, ,calni voice of Baron Grostof at that moment; and as he joined us the little woman winced and caught her breath, and came a little closer to me. I found myself wonder- ing what it meant—what she had been going to say, and whether he had overheard her. The incident produced a Most disgusting effect upon me, and as I had no chance of ques- tioning her then—for the Baron stayed with us, and only turned a discreet back for a couple of minutes while we said a hurried good-night—l was particularly thoughtful over my last cigar in the café that night. , "Bit hipped, Captain?" cried Donnisthorpe, who chanced to collie up when I was particularly preoccupied. \ "What do you know about that Baron Grostof ? " II asked, out of the fullness of my doubts. 1 He gave me one of his sharpest looks, and then „mused, while the two men he was with passed on ahead. He glanced very swiftly at the people around us, leant forward, and took up the wine' list from my table. "What wine are you drinking, Edwardes ? I'll shew you what's best. Here you are "—and he bent down very close to ins over the list, and put his finger at random on a wine as he whispered: "Russian spy—a couple of his men are two tables behind you "—then aloud: "That's it; Grosmont, my dear fellow, f '77; but mind it is the real '77. Good-night—aid bon voyage." He spoke gaily, and with a laugh went on to his companions. ' I turned to look at the men sitting at the table he had mentioned, and found them a couple of ordinary-looking Frenchmen, who were chattering, like most of the people in the place, about the game and comparing trente et guarante cards, on which the deals had been carefully pricked. Then I got up and went out of the place in dis- gust, and walked up and down the terrace, drinking in the cool, refreshing night air and thinking of Mignon, and wondering who the deuce the Baron was, and what he had really to do with her, and whether Donnisthorpe was right. But my thinking brought me no solution, though I wrestled half the night with tke problem. and was still worrying over it the next morning, in the lugubrious frame of mind in which a man leaves happiness for duty, when I started on my journey with my despatch for London. I was also specu- lating dolefully how long it would be before I Anould see Mignon again, and why she had not managed to turn out of bed that day early enough for us to have a word or tivo before I left. At Nice, however, I had a glorious surprise. Mignon was on the platform, with her maid, evidently going a journey, and I thought at first she looked pale. "This is awfully good of you! " I cried, rushing up td her, as soon as I could scramble out of my compartment. "How did you guess my train?" ' She started slightly at the question, but the red flush of happiness rushed into her face, and her ' eyes glowed with a light that illuminated ray troubled heart. . "I knew you were leaving Monte Carlo early, and guessed that your stay at Beaulieu would be short, so I came on here and waited. I felt I must see you." Her manner was nervous and catchy • and now that the flush had died out she lookea anxious and worried. "A nvtliinr" the matter? Nothing gone wrong, I hope? " I asked. She glanced up with a little catch of the breath. "No, but you are going away'; and I—l had a bad night." "Shall I put the things in the carriage, -nadame ? " asked the maid. "Are you going by this train? That's magnifi- rent," I cried. "Come along, this is my carriage_ l'ut them in here," I said to the girl. 'How far ye you going? I wish it was to London," I .-inspered. I.,ain going-home—to Cannes. And perhaps I'll go on a little further. I must tell you something " —she whispered this, although there was no one near us at the time. "When will you coins out again ? We must meet soon. If we don't, I am sure we shall never see eaeh other again." Her manner was certainly strange and restless, and I thought something serious must have occurred since the previous night. But the restless- ness wore off in the train, and it was a huge pleasure to me to think that this was due to her being with me. She told me nothing of such secrecy and importance as her manner had sug- gested, however. , By the time we reached Cannes she was laughing, o.nd appeared, much as usual, and was undecided whether to go on with me or not. She got out of the train, and we were standing together by the carriage door, when her maid came up for instruc- , tions. . "I won't go any further, Hugo," said Mignon, making her decision very suddenly, as it neenied to me; and the maid fetched her belongings out of the carriage. "And now, mind, my last word is— Wire me the instant you reach London, and then perhaps I shall have a surprise for you." I promised lier readily enotexh.. and tllen `l:ad ta
That satisfied feeling Comes after a dish of CUSTARD BLA.NC MANGE

wisliher good-bye. "T Minx that's your handker- chief on the seat there," I said, with a lame excuse. "Get in a moment aid fetch it." She understood me, and as the compartment was empty I followed and took her in my arms. Is was our only chance of saying good-bye properly. She clung to me very passionately,. "You love me, Hugo? and trust me? " "Absolutely, my datling," I whispered. "If you knew how I loved Sion! Good-bye--but there won't be many more gl-byes, I hope." "No. Not if you tru me." Those were her last words, for she had to scramble out hastily; and a moment later I was looking back to her as the train moved off, and she stood waving her mite of a handkerchief after I me.

I threw myself back on my seat to think, and hippy enoogh my thoughts were. Tat 2 o tons ro aeor ein ntiou pug omit dddrur eq I.trPtne3 I had lighted a Vngar. and was feeling for my note-book to look a little closely into the figures of my income, when ray eyes fell on my despatch case, which I had laid on the seat opposite me. It had , my name and everything on it, but in some way it I looked unfamiliar; and the moment I picked it up I saw it was a counterfeit made up to look like my own. I was the victim of a well-laid plot, and my despatch had been stolen. In an instant a hundred thoughts flashed on are of all that had happened during the last few days, with Donnisthorpe s warnings and suspicions as a bitter and pungent accompaniment. What should I do? That was the question. , A glance at my watch shewed are I had left Cannes about an hour and a half, and as not a _ _
soul but myserf had been in the compartment since then, it was clear that I must get back with the least possible delay, and commence the search from there.

I pulled the communicating cord therefore, stopped the train, and explained to the guard, who came up angry and gesticulating, something of what had happened. This calmed him, and he told me that two miles further on there was aimal,l station, where a returning express train could be stopped for me. One was due to pass in about an hour after we should reach there, and I spent the interval pacing Up and down the platform, wrestling with the ugly puzzle of the vanished despatches. I fought hard against the clamorous persistence of the thought that there was any connection between the event and Mignon's unexpected journey with the to Cannes; and I was infinitely angry with myself as the remembrance of her altered manner that morning would keep thrusting itself upon me, in company with the bitter recollection of Don- nistborpe's warning—that the Baron Grostof was a Russian spy. Whoever had served me this turn had ruined me. That was clear. I had proved myself incapable of performing my simple; easy duty, and I was unfit to retain my office. The thought was gall ' and bitterness, and I vowed that whoever had served me the trick should pay bitterly for it, if I found them—and behind the "whoever" were some of the darkest thbughts I have ever known. When I got back to Cannes I had another sur- prise. Young Donnisthorpe was sktting on the platform, \ smoking leisurely, and ivatching the arrival of the train.

"Hullo, you've been quick—back sooner than I expected. Been robbed ? " 'Yes; some thief has taken my despatch. But what--- Were you waiting for me? You don't mean you know anything about it already." "Don't know anything. Only guess. been so thick lately with those people." I turned a dark and threatening face on him. "All right; don't throttle me. I haven't in- sinuated anything. When did you have the 1 despatch last ?" "I had it at Nice all right." "Anyone in the carriage with you ? " "Yes, Madame Guislay," I said. I said it defiantly, and I think I'd have knocked him down if he'd suggested, even by a look, the suspicion which was buzzing and dinning, through my head. But he knew my mood, and kept off dangerous ground. "What have you come back to Cannes for?" "Hang you! I suppose you know," I said fiercely. "You know everything." "Do you suspect anybody?" he asked next. "No. How should I?" I flung the counter question at him. I tras sorely in need of someone to vent my anger on. Ile saw this, and said: "If it will do you any good, have a large and free swear at me. I can guess how mad you feel. it's an infernal shame to treat a man like this. May be an ugly business, too. But if you think I can help you, use me." "I don't want to swear at you," I said sullenly. "But I'd like ten minutes with the man who's done this."
You'vo
"Yes; man or woman, it's a cowardly trick." I knew what he meant, but didn't answer.

"Where are you going first ? " he added. "I should like to see you through with it. I'm afraid you've got a rough and tumble experience ahead! Unless you'd rather go up there alone? • "Where ? " I growled ungraciously. "There's only one place here, ,is there ? "We'll go together," I answered, angrily, my look stern and' dogged; and leaving the station we jumped into a cab, and I told the man to drive to the Villa Cora—Madame Guislay's. We didn't exchange a word in the carriage, but about a couple of hundred yards from the villa Donnisthorpe stopped the man, got out, paid him, and sent him back to the station. "What's this for? " I asked. "If you'll take my tip you won't let anyone know you've come back, and won't give their servants the trouble of announcing you. Round at the back we can get over---" "I'm not going to play the spy," I cried angrily. "All right, as you please—only you are on State sevice, you know; to say nothing of your own grievance. Besides, as the despatch has now been stolen, it's a Foreign Oflice job, and if you won't go in that way, I shall." "I'm not going to spy on the woman—to spy in such a case," I said, resolutely'. But I had been the first to refer thus openly to Mignon, and was wild with myself. "Man, you'd better face the truth, whatever it is."

But I would not give way, and I insisted upon entering the house from the front. He yielded, with a shrug of the shoulders, and we walked up .together. It chanced, however, that the gate of the villa was open, and that we found the front door also open. I insisted on ringing, but Donnisthorpe entered without any ceremony of the kind, and when no one came • in answer to my summons I grew • impatient.

A minute' later 'my • companion came darting noiselessly back to me, holding in his hand my despatch case—opened and empty. We exchanged a look, and I felt a pain like a cold, cramp death round my heart,. "Come, "'lie Whispered, seizing my wrist ; and I seemed no longer capable of resisting his stronge:- will.
. "W here was it? " I said, pointing to the case, which he:put down in the hall.

"In that room there," he replied under his breath, nodding towards the door of a room that I knew ta be Mignon's own sitting-room. I ground my teeth in impotent wrath. "Do you mean to suggest she put it there?" I aslad, savagely. "Be a mar,:" be said ; but his chief answer was a look. "Bonen-11er, we have to unearth this-- whoever it was."
"GO on, I said sullenly, beginning to feel that nci.bing mattered now.

lie put his finger to his lips, and led me as si eitlt hily as a cat into the room where he had found the case; then with another sign to me to be silent, he whisperei: "Listen." We stood in dead silence, and then I heard a sound that almost broke my heart. It was a woman's sob. Donnisthorpe's grasp tightened on my wrist, for I felt like a thief myself, and a scoundrel, for not making my presence known. The sob was repeated, and my heart leaped in response: Then came a sound of angry inipatience in,a_ruart's voice.

"Ugh! What's the good of that? You've done the test stroke of your life, practically made your forlune, and here you are whimpering and whining Lccaose you've had to deceive someone. The \wild's all deceit, fool." recognised the Baron's voice, but with the suavity gone out of it, and I could have found it in me to rush in and kick him for his brutality. lie had made her do it, no doubt, and now that remorse drove her to tears he behaved like a beast
c;:fe

-to her. ZZy arger against him was fast getting white hot. But I couldn't go on playing the eaves- dropper in the way which appeared' to please Loimisthorpe, and I was making for the door to ct.ter the room where the Baron and Mignon were, Let my companion Checked me with a vicious tug a my wrist. abe Btrcn spoke again. "I've done with this raw. he sr. and we heard the rustling of payers. "IN here's the case? Put the despatch back in it and then be oft.' Don't be a crying fool; no one «.ts you, vrd no one will suspect us either, if do :..s I told you. Take the train to FrOjus, wiun a.oot len miles out of Cannes pitch tho (OI of the wii,dow in the Erst tunnel you come to: then go back here as fast as you can. I'll make an es(rse for your absence. Give me the en n. Lai the girl murmured somethii.g c.,11141 not. I•-sit.—“ff.}ph it (lien. nat was 11:c moment Donnisthorpe chose to rush hi, and the suiprise that awaited me was only meeeelcd by the tremendous rush of relief that followed.

It was not Mignon at all, but her maid, who was closeted with the Baron, and when she saw lknnisthorpe rush for* atd and seize him, she first gt-re a scream, then turned to fly, and lastly, when icy big body blocked the way, she threw herself a her knees and began to sob out a confession. She was in the midst of it when Mignon entered, white and angry, with my despatch case in her hand.
"How comes this here? Ah, Hugo, you have brought it. But what is—what does all this mean? " she cried in dismay. And then I drew her to me and linked my arm in hers. I did not care what happened now.

The matter was soon explained to her by Donnis- thorpe, who kept quite cool all the time, and when be had finished she turned upon the wretched, grovelling maid. "And I thought you true to me, Annette! Go." Then to me: "You shall have the whole truth, Hugo; I care not who hears it. My uncle, there," set me on to rob you, pleading that I could render his country and France a service by getting him the despatches you carried. And I tried, but then I came to love you, dear "—she smiled to me— "and you can judge my terror lest you might learn my secret. He played upon that, and threatened to betray me to you. You remember there was something I wished to tell you, but dared not. I schemed to get you away this time safely to England, and thought I had done it—for I promised him I would rob you myself of the despatch—and I meant to follow you to England at once and tell you. But he has had a double scheme, and plotted with Annette here—this traitress." _ _

1 cared to her no more. Compared with the relief I experienced at her words, everything else was dwarfed, and my reply to Mignon was a smile of confidence and encouragement, while, I ran my arm round her waist and drew her to me and kissed her.

Then I took from her the despatch case, and put into it the papers from Baron's Grostof's table. "I am going to Beaulieu to explain matters," I said to Donnisthorpe. The latter stretched out a menacing forefinger at the Baron.

"I shall give you one., hour in which to prepare to start together for the Russian frontier, you and your accomplice here, and I'll send someone to see that you reach it," he said sternly. "And if you don't go you'll both be prosecuted for the theft. Just a word, Captain," he said to me, and we went out together. 'l'm going to Beaulieu to report this. You needn't bother unless you like; there won't be much row. The whole thing was just a trap laid to catch that greasy little beast in there ; and now that we've got him things can be made all right. I'm bound to say I feared to find someone else in it, and I'm thundering glad, for your sake, that she wasn't. If you take my tip you'll-go on to London as if nothing had happened. We can't make a row with Russia just now, and shall get rid of him quietly, as we wanted to."

fcriowed his advice and took my despatch on to London. But it was the last I ever carried for the Foreign Office, for Mignon went with me, and, as a result of our conferences on the way, I resigned as soon as I reached town.
A' couple of months later I entered another service, or, rather, Mignon and I entered it together, and a delightful one we have found it.
T- -1 Tux END.)

By ARTHUR W. MARCHMONT,
4uthor of "By Right of Sword," "A King for an

div.head: Hour," "A Dangerous Betrothal,"
div.p: Hour," "A Dangerous Betrothal,"

I love the gardens of Old Monaco to this hour in remembrance of that one April evening, ,and if E close my eyes I can call up the scene at will. We were standing, Mignon and I, in one of the Driel-shaped embrasures of the wall, looking down it the blue sea far below, where the waves were tapping, with a caressing murmur, the rocks at the base; and the golden glory of the sunset, the deal :weetness of the air, the scent of the flowers, all 7orne back to me, mingled with the soft, subtle ?.ssence which spread itself from the tiny lace handkerchief which Mignon waved laughingly to the occupants of a boat which was just rounding the point.

/ I The sound of her musical laugh was ravishment, snd the love-light in her eyes was the sweetest ; thing I had ever seen, as she turned fo me and, after glancing round in smiling alarm to make sure no one was near to disturb us, came nestling to my side, to press my hand, sigh in sheer abandonment of pleasure, and lay her head against me. The touch of her hair magnetised me, and I had no thought save of how much I loved her. I had ,only just told my love and listened to the intoxicating confession that she returned it, and for all that late afternoon and evening we roamed the gardens together, and I was as happy as a lover ould be, with never a thought for any coming trouble. Indeed, there did not Erin room in the world for such a thing as trouble. "Life shall be a dream, Hugo," she whispered once, "a long, sweet, happy dream. Ali, how I have wished for this!" "You have thought of me a bit, then, while I've been away," I said, with the fatuous pleasure of a lover at clearing 'her speak of her love. "I hate your Foreign Office," she said, with I pretty energy which found expression in a foot-tap and a frown. "Why hate the Foreign Office, little woman?" I asked, smiling. "Because it takeeyou away from me, big man." She lifted her head from my shoulder to smile up to me at this epithet. lam tall. "You'll have to change that feeling, Mignon; it helps me to live." I as a Queen's Messenger, and, as the Foreign Office chief was at his Beaulieu villa, I had been running backwards and forwards a good deal lately. It was in these jaunts I had renewed my acquaintance with Mignon—Madame Guislay—a lovely girl widow, whose villa at Cannes was like a lode-stone to me. I had only come out the previous evening, and had heard, to my delight, that she and her uncle, the Baron Grostof, a Russian, were staying for a few days at Monte Carlo. I had three days off duty, and had already made the most of one of them. "I never shall change, if it keeps us apart," she said, with a frown on her tell-tale face. "And yet—" She began with a smile and then stopped. "And yet what? " She glanced round as if suddenly nervous. "If it had not been for your Foreign Office I ihould never have known you." That was rather an odd thing for her to say, I thought, because, as. a fact, I had made the acquaintance of the uncle—a man I disliked cordially—at the Hotel de Paris and in the play rooms a long time before, and it was he who had introduced me to Mignon, and had taken me over to the Cannes villa and started the friendship. "Why the Foreign Office, Mignon ? " I asked. She looked up at me and smiled, and then, some- how, the light of the smile seemed to go out of the face, though the features retained the form of it. "Do you guess how much I really love you, Hugo? " she asked, with what seemed sweet irrelevance. " I hope so, sweetheart," I said, and drew her closer to me. Then I found she was trembling. "And you trust me ever so much?" "So much that nothing could change me." "Ah!" It was a sigh of deep happiness; then, after a long pause, she said: "I should like to put you. to.a test.:

She laughed as if in mischief, but there was a wistfulness in her tone that somehow seemed to strike me, though I am neither very observant or quick. "I should not be afraid of it," I answered quietly. "But these times are too prosaic for any- thing of that sort, end I don't think, somehow, you would care to impose any too cruel a test; you'd be afraid of my being hurt." "I don't mean that, and she turned and stared straight out across the sea. "I ' mean a test of faith, not endurance."

"I think I should conic out on top, even at that," said I, smiling. - She looked wonderingly and lovingly at me then, but made, no answer in words, only smiled in response to my smile and moved close to me. Then some people came up and disturbed us. We moved away, and soon afterwards walked back, lingering and love-making. down into the Condamine, past the harbour, and up the hill to Monte Carlo, where we_Larted.

When 1 bad finished my dinner an hour or two later. and sat smoking and waiting for the time at which I was to meet Mignon again, young Donnis- thorpe came and sat by me, puffing his cigarette with that air of shrewd wisdom which attaches of his kind a:ect,

"Pleasant up in the old gardens to-day?" he asked presently, looking keenly at his cigarette to avoid the glance of surprise I could not quite repress. How the'dence the fellow got; his information I never could tell, but he seemed to know every;, thing. "1 suppose it was," I answered indifferently. "So do I,* he said, with a dry, irritating laugh. "She's a very beautiful woman—girl, indeed, though she has been married. I suppose you know Potbelly was taking a careful note of the proceedings? " . .
By this repulsive term he was accustomed to describe the Baron Grost6f.

"Proceedings? " I echoed. "He takes a lot of interest in you, Captain," and Donnisthorpe let out a sharp, shrewd, infinitely suggestive glance. that flashed for just a second into my eyes. "I should look out." His manner implied such superior worldly wisdom that it irritated me, though I longed to ask him what he meant, and also what he knew about the Baron. But I held my tongue and smoked vigorously in silence. "By the way, have you insured your life?" he asked next.

"What the deuce do you mean? "I asked testily. "I must say that's one point I like about you, Edwardes. You never pretend to see a thing when, RS a matter of fact, you don't see it—and that's pretty often, by the way." "I suppose yea know what you're driving at, but I'll be hanged if I d 0.," He laughed that dry little laugh again. "Ali, you big, good-lOoking six-footers don't need to see things ; muscle carries You- through. But you mustlook out, and even you won't mind a hint. There's an awful hunger just now in Russia to get hold of the Foreign Office secrets about the China business, and, as there are a lot of confidential payers travelling backwards and forwards between the old man at Beaulieu ,and Downing-street, you fellows who carry them should he spry. Some of these Russian Johnnies don't stick at much. That's what I mean about insuring your life, thouoah I don't know that they would go as far as that."

"Oh, they're not likely to try that kind of .game on with said I, with the confidence born of big muscles. "They don't always rely on strength. A man in love has more-vulnerable points than his muscles, don't you know." "What d'xe mean ? " I cried quickly. "You don't mean to insinuatc--" But I stopped, for the mere thought was treachery to Mignon, and I think I'd have broken anyone's head who bad dared to say a word against her. "My dear Captain, you'd half kill me with a single grip of those great brawny hands of yours if I were such a fool as to insinuate anything of the kind. But you're not in love with Pot-belly, at any rate." "Look here, Donnisthorpe, this makes mighty unpleasant hearing for me. Madame Guislay has to-day done me the honour to coment to be my wife, and I'm not going to hear things against her or hers."
I "Phew!" he whistled, then, after a pause, he said: "Well, she's a lovely woman, as lovely a woman as I've ever seen. and. no doubt, you're a

div.head: DUST PROBLEM IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: DUST PROBLEM IN CHESHIRE.
Watering Would Cost £40,799.
EXPENDITURE OF VO PER MILE
PROPOSED.
Cheshire is still struggling with the motor car dust problem.

For the watering of all the roads of the country in such complete fashion.as to eliminate the nuisance it is officially estimated that an expenditure of not less than £40,799 would have to be incurred. Of that sum £11,324 would be required for plant, and £29,475 for labour and water. The expenditure on plant simply for the main trunk roads most used by motorists would be :- 47 Water carts at £5O each 42 Stand pipes, at £7 each 29.1 31 Pumps, at £2O each 620 1131 Miles of roads to be watered for 100 days per annum, including team labourand cost of water 6,810

L 10,074 Apart from the great financial responsibility involved it is very doubtful, in the opinion of the county sur- veyor,whether sufficient water could be obtained during the dry summer months, when pits and brooks have to depended upon. The dust-laying experiments which have been made from time to time during the past two years in several of the urban districts, so far as the informa- tion of the assistant county surveyor goes, have not been generally satisfactory, having regard to the cost incurred. In Mr. Holland's opinion until some permanent remedy is discovered, tempo- rary relief must be looked for in the direction of increased judicious cleaning and watering, the extra cost of which will be £4,850 or approximately £4O per mile.

The Main Roads Committee of the County Council is equally at a loss. They are not prepared to recom- mend the Council to incur what they describe as the enormous cost of the watering remedy, nor do they think that particular lengths of road should be dealt with.

When these decisions were arrived at, it was further resolved to do nothing pending the issue of the report of the Royal Commission. That document has made its appearance, but it is doubtful whether the Main Roads Committe will receive from it any assistance towards a solution of the problem they rind so puzzling.

div.head: Latchford Drowning Fatality.
div.p: The Latchford Drowning Fatality.

Mr. S. Brighouse conducted an inquiry at the War- rington Police Statim on Tuesday into the death of a girl named Margaret Stirrup, the seven-year-old daughter of Charles Stirrup, painter, 400, Knutsford- road, Warrington, who was drowned in the Bridge- water Canal, near Black Bear Bridge, Latchford, on Thursday last. The deceased was playing on the ' canal bank with two other companions, and whilst in the act of reaching some flowers from Lear thewater's edge she overbalanced and fell into the water. Before assistance could be summoned she sank, and the body was recovered shortly afterwards by a tram driver !named Warburton.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."
