div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
AUGUST 4th 1906.

The subject of Professor E. "THE RAY LANKEsTER'S opening FAIRY TALES address to the annual meet OF SCIENCE." ing of the British Associa- tion was happily suggested to him by the occasion on which it was to be delivered. The first meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science was held in York seventy-five years ago. Fifty years later the members assembled in the same city to 'celebrate a notable jubilee. What could be more natural or appropriate than that, in the present year, the Association sh.ould meet in the ancient Eboracum, the most recently destroyed of the Roman towns in this country, to survey its past and to look into its future, from the point on which it first began to coruscate, or that its President should choose as the subject of his address the advance which science has made during the last quartet .f a century F Dr. RAy LANEESTER is neither a great enthusiast nor a great discoverer. He is a type of the hard, practical, solidly-founded Man, who takes nothing on trust, and who does not carry his theories beyond the limits of his proofs. Professor LODGE, Sir WILLIAM CROOBES, and others have carried their researches into the domains of the supernatural. He thinks none the better of them for that. He regards scientific investigation as a prospector regards a newly-discovered gold- reef. He values it accordingly as the samples turn out. If we wish to know something on the psychical side of science he is not the man to turn to. Science has no psychical side for him. He wants the solid fact " down on the nail "; but for that reason he is all the more qualified to become the historian of what is indisputable, of what is unquestioned advance in scientific investi- gation and knowledge, of a brief but thrilling

period in which more strange but confirmed facts of science have been discovered than in all the years that intervened between the last meeting of the British Association at York and the last days of Aristotle.

We may begin our notice of Professor RAY LANKESTER'S address by summing it up. It is a quite successful contention that scientific progress is not a series of accidents, but a sequence of dis- coveries. To state the case in another way, " the fairy tales of science and the long results of Time are not differing things, as Tennyson seems to have supposed, but the same. Oae discovery is the con- sequence of another : the final result may be a revelation. Coming to the knowledge of hitherto unknown things has been the char- acteristic of the science of the last twenty - five years, and Professorßav LANKESTER shews us how one discovery has spring out of ianother, and what new conclusions are forced upon us as a result. "There is continuity and healthy evolu- tion in the realm of science," he says, He is alluding, of coarse, to the X-rays and to radium, which have upset all manner of scientific ideas and theories,and have compelled us to think differently —and to a surprising extent differently—of the universe. Professor RAY LANKESTER'S object is to shew how one discovery helps us on to another, how progress means still further progress,and how the achievements of one man, or of one set of men, are merely "stepping stones to higher things." He remarks that " there can be no doubt that the past quarter of a century will stand out for ever in human history as that in which new chemical elements, not of an ordinary type, but possessed of truly astounding properties, were made known with extraordinary rapidity and sureness of demon- stration." But the knowledge of radio-activity— and it is that to which he alludes—came gradually and not in a rush ; though undoubtedly with some swiftness. Let us look at the successive steps. Five inert gaseous elements were 'discovered by RAYLEIGH and RAMSAY. Lord RAYLEIGH found that there is present in the atmos- phere a one per cent. of something which had passed for oxygen. This is argon, so named because of its inertness. But even this one percent. was impure, for Ramsay, as the I next step, obtained three new gaseous elements from it. Then he discovered something more, and of vastly more imporGant moment, which was that a further new gaseous element, helium, is identical with something which exists in the sun Ein enormous quantities. There followed the dis- covery of radium, from which helium. proved to be a gaseous'enianation.lThe alchemist's dream, if not realised, was at least justified, Professor RAY LANKESTER thinks. Here was an actual and natural transmutation of metals. One °talent could be observed in the process of transmuting itself into another.

What, however, are some of the conclusions that we may draw from the existence of this newly discovered element:? Here are some facts to pro ceed upon. Professor RAY LANKESTER says : "Even a small quantity of radium diffused through the earth will suffice to keep up its temperature against all loss by radiation." Then, radium has the quality of renewing itself. Seeing that it can do what Professor RAY L &NEES= says,there is an end of the theory that the earth is a cooling globe. Even more important must be the conclusions as regards the sun. A theory that has been recently much in fay- our with nann of science is one which con tends that the sun maintains its heat by its Own compression, or shrinking. The extinction of its heat, if this were the case, would only be a matter of time, though the time were measured by many millions of years. But the helium which is an emanation of the radium exists in the sun in vast quantities, and this, as Professor RAY LANKESTER remarks, upsets " all the calculations of physicists as to the duration in past and future of the sun's heat and the temperature of the earth's surface." It upsets, also, all calculations of geological time. Not long ago it was common:to spetur of 35,000,000 of years as the age of the world. The period has since been extended by men like Lord KELVIN to 1,000,000,000 of years. The discovery of radium extends the period backward and forward to an illimitable and, therefore unimaginable extent. We must now, even from the point of view of physical science, look from eternity into eternity.

Space will not permit us to say much more of Professor RAY LANKESTER'S deeply suggestive but quite unpretentious address. Tne last twenty-five years have seen the birth of the Becquerel and the X-Rays, of photography as we'know it, of new and previously unimagined means of dealing with disease, and, in fact, of a new conception of science. Vast has been in that period our accumulation of what Professor RAYLANKESTER calls "gathered fact and growing generalisation." Is science extinguish- ing the mystery of the world, of the universe, of human existence? Is the "fairy tale" at an end ? Has poetry been strangled by the hydra of new knowledge ? Far to the contrary. The mystery has been extended and deepened. The fairy tale has spread itself from the simple to the multiplex; the imagination of the poet never had so wide and grand and mysterious an area in which to extend itself. Only the poet is wanting.
Some time ago, an ingenious THE WEATHER. littie book was published on

the art of conversation. This was regarded as a game of chess. There were all kinds of openings which could be made safely, and, according to the replies received, so could questions follow. It was promised that such subjects as religion or politics, on which people are apt to quarrel, should be avoided. The weather: was considered safe. It appealed to rich and poor, aristocrat and democrat alike. A random observation that the weather was bad, bright, changeable, clear, close, cold, damp, dry, dull, fine, rainy, rough, serene, steady, stifling, stormy, warm, wet, or windy, could lead on to a wealth of verbal intercourse and an outpouring of soul worthy of Demosthenes. Instead of railing against our variable climate, therefore, many people should be thankful that it is so changeable. A ruddy sunset and a grey or misty sunrise can be talked about poetically, if a schoolgirl remembers her 011endorf, for quite a' long while. If the weather fails, a useful plan is to take topics alphabetically. This is easy. Begin with the letter A. The question, "Do you like asparagus ? " of course leads up to talk of other nutritious herbs, and possibly of lilies, since the asparagusgbelongs to ' the lily family. But when the letter B is tackled,the debutante should be beware of Bananas especially if her partner is somewhat deaf. The story of the bashful maiden who had successfully alluded to the Albert Hall, when sitting next an old Anglo-Indian colonel who always called bananas plantains, is well known. He did not catch what she said. She repeated her question. In a louder voice he explained that he was hard of hearing. The general conversation stopped. Blushing, the young lady again said, " Do you like bananas ?" "Oh no, my dear,"came the stentorian reply, "I prefer the old-fashioned nightgown."

div.p: A.LDER'MEN.

Are aldermen really muni- cipal assets? This is a question which naturally arises to the mind on learning that the Manchester City Council has resolved to petition Parliament in favour of an alteration of the municipal Corporations Act to make aldermen subject to popular election. At present, " once an Alderman, always an Alderman" is a stock phrase. In nearly all municipalities the only qualification for succession to the high office is seniority, which, of course operates almost auto- matically. flow long does it take the gentlemen who has become alderman by seniority to become merely a cypher by senility? Not always a very longtime! Referring to the thirty-one aldermen on the Manchester City Council, the "Evening Chronicle "is brutally frank, not to say rude. Of these thirty-one, it says, " an intelligent observer could count—almost on the fingers of one hand, easily upon the fingers of both—the fu,l list of those who are in any sense an assistance in the government of the city." This should cause a certain amount of introspection among Manchester aldermen. In Warrington too, there have been holders of aldermanic seats who have become like barnacles on the bottom of a ship—more of an encumbrance than anything else. An alderman has his uses, of cburse, and the office is not altogether unneces- sary. It is a fitting reward for valuable public service, but it should not become the bourne where the ratepayers cease from troubling and the weary public servant is at rest. Aldermen weild a large proportion of the power on a borough or city council, and they should be responsible to the ratepayers rather more directly than at present. We do not imagine that the Manchester resolution will result in any great stirring among the law-makers at Westminster— it may very probably be rescinded at an early date —but it will have done good in drawing phblic attention to the fact that the sort of royal reign to which Aldermen succeed is not the intention of the Act, nor is it conducive to the wisest and most conscientious local government.

This week there have been CoNscrENTious two cases before the War- OBJECTORS. r i ngt on magistrates of applications by "conscienti- ous objectors" for vaccination exemption certifi- cates. Two cases—two decisions, one man granted an exemption and the other refused. On Monday the applicant was questioned by two or three members of the "great unpaid," but as he stuck to his opinion that vaccination would be detrimental to the health of his child, the Magistrates' Clerk advised that that was sufficient, and the certificate was granted. On Wednesday, the second appli- cant fared much worse with an even stronger case. He professed to have lost a child through vaccina- tion, but this oely appeared to arouse the ire of the chairman, Mr. Charles White who is a medical man of long experience. He refused to sign the order and treated the poor applicant rather harshly Now, if this man had made his statement before. Monday's bench he would have got his exemption but owing to the refusal of Dr. White to administer the law as he finds it,he will have to go to the further expense and trouble of making a fresh application. We have sympathy with Dr. White's attitude on the vaccination question ; his conscientious objec- tion to granting certificates of exemption probably could not be stronger,but this does not alter the fact that as a magistrate he has a duty to perform,how- ever repugnant it may be. Apparently the Home Secretary's recent circular for the guidance of magistrates on this very question has not had much effect. Yet the circular specifically points out that " the question for magistrates is not whether the applicant's belief is well-founded or ill-founded, but solely whether they are satisfied that he con - conscientiously believes that vaccination win be prejudicial to the health of the child in question." If a man honestly avows his conviction to this effect it should suffice to get him his certificate of exemption. Thoso magistrates who are so prejudiced in favour of vaccination that they cannot bring themselves to carry out the provisions of the Act should refrain from adjudicating on vaccination cases when there is another " J.P.' available. The sort of "justice" which has been meted out from the Warriuge Court of late is likely to bring the English osig's. tracy into disrepute.

-- Just now when inter' A LITTLn BILL national :Parliamentarians FOR FRANCE. are engaged in the discus- sion of the evils and expenses of war, we are reminded opportunely by the appearance of the British Embassy Report cn the French Budget that not only war but even the rumour of war is expensive. The maintenance of armies and navies is bad enough, but when a "scare "comes, although it passes quickly enough it leaves the country concerned considerably the poorer for the visitation. Take the Morocco scare of last veer, when France did not know the moment when Berlin might " loose" upon her. The Budget of 1907 will have to meet the cost of the prepara- tions which had to be made in haste in the emer- gency-7a little sum of £8,000,000, which will have to be defrayed by a loan: Other scar3s have been likewise expensive. The Fashoda business ran this country and Franca into a tidy little sum, though it did not, fortunately, involve us in war. Another abortive but necessary expenditure was that on the flying squadron which was ordered out after William ll.'s teleßram to President Kruger over the Jameson Raid. Still, all these things if they do cost money have their uses. In some eases they prevent the greater waste of war, and anyhow it is difficult to see when a country seems in danger of attack how she is to avoid the cost of prepar

"it is on the banks of the PROPHETS OF WOE. Neva, the Vistula, and the Volga that the fate of New Europe and of the future of humanity is being decided," says M. Anatole France in a preface which he has written for a book which has just been published in France by a Russian journalist on the origin and history of the pogroms, "the official incitements to massacre." One does not forget the propl;sesies of strikes and Jewish massacres which have been made for the coming week-end, nor—as a thing of wider significance— the warning of the old Socialist Bebel to the German deputies, "Do not forget that the revolutionary storm which has now broken out in Russia finds an echo in the heart of the German working man." This is the potent and far-reaching significance of it all. The " Times " says of Russia's coming experience: "The cataclysm will shake many things far beyond her frontiers." M. Anatole France sees in the threatened conflict the old historic struggle between Czardom,or Clesarisni, and the proletariat. He appeals for the sympathy of the French proletariat. Czar and Cmsar are the same word and the terrible meanings of each are identical. The Russian proletariat have already exercised a decisive influence on the destinies of the world ; but he asks, as massacre after massacre is surveyed and pogrom after pogrom, how long will this fury of Czardom continue ?
J. WALKER & CO.

Coming Events. The twelfth annual show in connection with the Hatton Horticultural Society will be held on Thurs- day at Hatton Hall, and will be opened by Mrs. Henry Greonall. He will enter the town via Knutsford road and proceed to the Town Hall where he will be welcomed by the Mayor. A public meeting will be held in the evening at which the General will deliver an address on " The secret of the success of the Salvation Army." Mr. H. Thornton will preside. We have in course of preparation the first issue of "The Warrington Football Annual and Sports Record" which we hope to make an absolutely indis- pensable encyclopmdia of sport for all local sportsmen. All other " annuals " of this kind are general in their interest—ours will appeal specially to Warrington people. in its GO pages will be found a short history of the Warrington Football Club, the first team and " A " team fixtures, Northern League fixtures, War- rington Association Football League fixtures, the fixtures of local junior clubs, including Walker's Brewery, numerous interesting football records con- nected with the Warrington Club, Cup-tie chronicles (Rugby and Association), running, swimming, and cycling records, and a list of secretaries' addresses which will cover all athletic clubs of all kinds in Warrington. The annual will also contain portraits of the Warrington "A" team, C. Berry (local champion cyclist), C. J. Straw (cross-country champion) and T. P. Bradshaw (.the pioneer of local Association football). 1 Junior Conservative Picnic. , The members of the Warrington Junior Conserva- tive Association and their friends, to the number of 700, on Tuesday spent the evening driving through the country around Warrington. Seventeen 'buses were engaged and as the weather was beautifully fine the drive round Lymm was greatly enjoyed.

_ STILL LEADING, the "HERALD" KITCHEN RANGES and " PEVERIL " FIRE GRATES Sole Agent.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. Accident at Latchford Locks. About half-past seven on Saturday morning, a young man named William Smith, 10, -Cooper-street, Runcorn, who is employed on the tug boat Minnie, was mooring the boat at latchford locks when his leg was caught between the rope and a capstan. The limb was badly crushed and broken, and Smith was conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary in the horse ambulance.

Canal Burst at Lymm. The ocene of the Bridgewater Canal burst at Agden, Lymm, was visited during the week-end by thousands of people from the surrounding districts. Anglers have enjoyed good sport in landing the thousands of small fish which were left in the shallow water in the two miles stretch of the canal which had to be drained in order to allow the damage being. made good. Directly after the water had been dammed at Lymjn Bridge and Agden Bridge, on Friday afternoon, an 3 the water drained off by means of the sluices, a gang of about thirty workmen under Mr. Wiswall, of Runcorn, engineer to the company, set about the task of repairing the damage, and on Saturday evening commenced rebuilding the wall at Agden with Runcorn and stone. This was completed by Monday, when the water was let in again and traffic resumed. The wall is two feet thick, and seven and a half high. Re Alfred Stanway Limited. The Vice-Chancellor of the Palatine Court at Man- chester (Mr. 0. Leigh Clare), on Monday last made an order by consent staying proceedings in the debenture holders' action on terms agreed upon. Mr. Eastwood (instructed by Mr.T. R. Roberts) appeared for the trustee for debenture 'aolders,and Mr. Gordon Hewart (instructed by Messrs. H. B. White & Sons), appeared for the official liquidator. A petition for the com- pulsory winding up of the company was made by the County Court Judge at Warrington on 22nd February ' 1906 whereupon the official receiver in bankruptcy I became he official liquidator. All the assets were claimed by the debenture holders, who had commenced an action to enforce their security. The official liquidator, however, discovered that the debentures were not validly issued and accordingly the action was stayed,and an order made by consent, under which the holders of the debentures will rank as Ordinary creditors, and the assets, after payment of the remuneration and costs of the Receiver and of the costs of the trustee for the debenture holders, will be transferred to the official liquidator for the benefit of the ordinary creditors. The Padgate-lane Burglary. At the Liverpool Assizes on Saturday before Mr. Justice Kennedy, Samuel Simkiss and James Green- wood, both of Ashton-under-Lyne, were charged with burglarionaly breaking and entering the dwelling- house of William Court, Padgate-lane, Poulton, between the 25th and 26th of June, and stealing three gold rings, one brass ring, a brass watch, two pairs of b6ots, two pairs of socks, a pocket book, a club card, 30 packets of cigarettes, 3s. in cash, and a money box, of the total value of SA. Mr. Greaves Lord prose- cuted. The evidence was to the effect that on the morning of the 20th of June, Mr. Court noticed the scullery window was wide open, and there was a piece of glass on the floor. He examined the house and found that the articles named in the charge were missing. The prisoners had been arrested by Sergt. Mellor.—His Lordship remarked that prisoners had been wandering about the country stealing instead df working. There were twelve petty convictions against Sioakiss, who was now sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment with hard labour. Greenwood was sent to gaol for twelve months with hard labour. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—AdFL.

Warrington Agricultural Show. The seventeenth annual show of the Warrington and District Agricultural Society will be held in Walton Park on Thursday, 16th August. Prize's, cups, &c., are affered to the value of about £7OO. As in past years, Sir Gilbert Greensll, Bart., gives a district champion cup value £lO and two silver cups value £5 each. Mr. F. Stapleton Bretherton gives a special prize value £5, and the ,vice-president, Lord Lilford, a silver cup value £5, while Lady Greenall offers three special prizes of £2 each to the blackstnith for the best shod horse which has been regularly shod at the same forge during the six months or I thereabouts previous to the date of the show, in certain specified classes! Mr. J. Whittaker Kenworthy, Mr. James Gould, Messrs. Henry Milling and Co., and Messrs. Day and Sons also offer special prizes. Medals lamreporffovereenadenb the ieStyhie,randHtohrseeHSaocckineetyy, HtohreseHsuonciteetrys: Messrs. Ainscough also give special prizes for shire , mares stinted to and for foals got by their shire stallion " Ambush." There are classes for shires, hunters, hackneys, harness horses, jumpers, trades- men's or tenant farmers' tignouts, cattle, pigs, cheese and butter. A special fedture of the show will be novice classes in the open hunter and open harness classes for horses not having previously won large prizes at other shows.

Oddrellowshlp. The half,yearly meeting of the " Prince of Wales " Lodge (Manchester Unity) of Oddfellows was held at the Pelican Hotel, Bro. Maddock presiding. There was a good attendance of members, together with Prov. G.M., T. P. Bradshaw and Prov. D.G.M., Wm. Holbrook. The accounts for the past half-year, ending June 30th, were submitted by the Secretary (P.G. Thomas Wadsworth). They showed that the total receipts amounted to £409 108. 4d., including £53 17s. interest on investments. Tile total expendi- ture was £317 9s. 4d., including £163 13s. 4d. dis- tributed in sick pay, and £5 is. Id. in benevolent and other grants to members in distress, &T. There is a balance on the sick fund of £3,161 IGs. on the management fund of £22 7s. Old., and on the benevo- lent fund of £5 9s. 8!cl. The total worth of the Lodge is now £3,193 11s. 9d. The membership of the Lodge at the end of June was 478. After the ordinary business, the Secretary, at the request of the meeting, gave a short, summary of the five years. Quinquennial returns recently compiled by the Lodge for the Actuary of the Order for valuation purposes. Several members expressed themselves pleased with the progress made, and the sound financial position of the Lodge. A vote of thanks was passed to the Lodge officers and Bro. Maddock for presiding.

Sl-GUINEA CYCLES. Excellent value. Call and inspect.—J. S.GARLAND,SI to 55, Bridge-st.—Advt Warrington Rural District Council. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wed- nesday, when there were present : Mr. Brooks (Presiding), Dr. Murray, G-. Mather, J. W. Knowles, W. Houghton, J. Backhouse, R. Forshaw, J. C. Sutton (clerk). S. Sutton (assisiant clerk), B. G. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assisrant surveyor); F. W. Kerfoot (inspector) and Dr. Sephton (medical officer.) The Medical Officer reported that during the month there had been 23 births and 22 deaths. The death rate was equal to 22.0 per 1000 as against 30.0, the average of the past three months, and 22.0 for the corresponding period of last year. Of the deaths 12 occurred in the County Asylum, Winwick, exclusive of which the death rate proper for the district was 00 per 1000. Only one case of scarlet fever (at Sankey) had been reported during the year.—Dr. Sepliton said he had received complaints as to the water supply at Pear Tree Farm, Houghton. The farm belonged to the Corporation and he recommended that the Corporation be given notice to supply the water.—Mr. Knowles : Such a notice has been given before and the Corporation defy us.— Dr'. Sephton said he had received a copy of the quarterly report from Dr. Sergeant, Country Medical Officer. Warring- ton Rural District was second on the list as regarded lowness of mortality. Their figures for the quarter were 96 deaths per 1000 with no deaths under the zymotic class. The lowest on the list was Lunesdale where the death rate was 8.6 per 1000.

Warrington Student's Success. At the recent technological examinations held at the Liverpool Technical Institute, Mr. E. Spann, son of Mr. R. Spann, coachbuilder, Warrington' was successful in obtaining the City of Guilds of London Institute silver medal and first prize, the highest award in Great Britain for cart and van building. Local Athletic Successes. Two of the prizes offered at the Liverpool N.C.U. sports on Saturday were carried off by Warrington Athletes. In the novice mile race A. Powell (scratch) arrived home third whilst in the quarter mile championship the third place was obtained by A. Howard. At the Salford Police Sports on Saturday, C. Berry, of Warrington, was third in the half-mile scratch race, following home two clever riders in E. Payne, of Worcester, and J. Harvey, of Stoke. Registration. • 1 It is important that all persons entitled to vote should ascertain that their names have been placed on the register, as neglecting to do so may result in their disfranchisement. Copies of the register can be seen at all Churches and Chapels and public buildings in the town and at the General Post Office. Persons with the necessary qualifications and whose names are wrongly omitted should communicate with Mr. J. Howes, jun., at the Liberal Club before August 20th.

PREMIER CYCLES, 7,8, 10, 12 and 14 guineas Cash or 18 monthly payments. Sole agent, J. S. • GARLAND, 51, 53 and 55, Bridge-st.—Advt. Poor Children's Camp. The children of Warrington highly appreciate the opportunity afforded for a holiday at the seaside by the camp at Prestatyn, and last week-end over 100 delighted girls arrived in Warrington after a week on the Welsh coast. The second batch of girls left War- rington on Monday for a week by the sea and moun- tains. Lovely weather has been experienced, and the time has been spent going walks, playing cricket &c., and in the water. Most of the children want to stop another week, so thoroughly is the holiday enjoyed. Next week it will be the poor boys' turn to occupy the camp. LAWN TEIsTNIS, CROQUET, and other outdoor sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge-st.—Advt. Music in the Park. - - .

The League of the Cross Band will play the following programme in the Park on Sunday under the conductorship of Mr. T. Hynes :—Hymn," 0 Sacred Heart," arranged by J. Frost ; march, "Unique," J. H. White ; selection, " Moses in Egypt," Rossme ; song, " Sing me to sleep," soloist, D. Mahoney, E. Green; selection, " Galaxy of Beauties," Round ; selection, " Gems of operatic melody," Round; "God save the King." The above band will also play on Thursday evening. Theft of Brass. At Warrington on Thursday,James Birchall,Watkin- street, was charged with stealing a shilling's worth of brass from Dallam Forge. Mr. P. G. Taylor, who prosecuted on behalf of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles said that the prisoner had been in the employ of the company for thirty years, and they were very sorry to have to prosecute him but the thefts from the works had been so continuous ;hat they were obliged to take proceedings. The prisoner was seen on Wednesday in Scotland-road by Superintendent Monaghan, who noticed that his pockets were bulky. Prisoner was arrested whilst offering the brass for sale. The magistrate imposed a fine of Ils, and costs (£1 95.) or fourteen days. J, R. WOOD Piano Dealer and Tuner, 47, Old London-road.; Stockton Heath.—Advt. Peerless Patents Company. At the Warrington Bankruptcy Couit, on Friday, , Samuel Booth, 43, Walton-road, Stockton Heath, builder's merchant, trading as the Peerless Patent Co., Bridge Foot, appeared for his public examination in bankruptcy. The statement of affairs disclosed gross liabilities of £2,750 16s. lid. and liabilities expected to rank for divi- dend of £1,178 4s. Bd. The assets are estimated to realize £37 7s. 9d., leaving a deficiency of £1,140 Ns. 11d. Bankrupt, who says he became aware of his insolvency in May 1906, attributes his failure to bad trade, bad debts, heavy business ex- penses, and the non payment by a limited Company of part of the purchase money for the business. The examination was adjourned. Richmond's Firemen's Picnic.

That good workers make good players was further exemplified on Saturday when the firemen forming the A and B Brigades in conneetion with the Warrington works of the Gas Stove and Meter Company had their second annual outing. The destination chosen was the Bridge Inn,Gateacre,where the firemen accompanied by a number of guests arrived in gowl :time after a very pleasant drive. The cycling coa.tingent which had started much later was not far behind. Next to

the dinner, the principal event of the afternoon was a bowling main confined to members of the Brigades. The bowlers were quickly on the green and though the rain, which came on shortly afterwards, wet their coats, it did not damp their enthusiasm for the game, which was played to a finish whilst the visitors had a merry time with music, &c.,in the pavilion where they had retired for shelter. The successful competi- tors in the bowling were :—T. Edelsten, Ist prize ; WT. Kirk, 2nd prize ; W. Wrench, 3rd prize ; J. Barnes, 4th prize ; W. Nicholson, Ist Consolation ; J. Hogan, 2nd Consolation. At dinner ample justice was done to the catering and after the usual loyal toasts, distribution of prizes, &c., a smoking concert was held in the pavilion with Mr. Burnett (superintendent of the brigades) in the chair. The following able volunteers contributed to the pro- gramme :—Me.ssrs. J. R. Burnett, H. Hill, W. Pater- son, J. Birchall, D. Witton, T. Ed ' elsten, J. Leslie J. Hogan, A. 13radley, the accompanist being Mr. W. Pemberton. Votes of thanks to the chairman and to the artistes brought the proceedings to a close, and the weather having cleared, the return journey was made under the happiest conditions, Warrington being reached shortly after 11 o'clock. Thursday saw the opening of the Royal Lancashire Agricultural Society's annual show, at Lancaster. which is to be continued over to-day, to-morrow, and Monday (Bank Holiday). It is almost two decades ago that the society last visited the ancient town, and the first commanding thought is of the wonderful strides not only in the progress of the society but in the advance of agriculture in its various branches. The total entries show a considerable advance on that of any previous yek and the quality of the exhibits reaches a high standard. Council Meeting Postponed. In consequence of several members of the Council being absent from town on Tuesday next the Council meeting fixed for that day has been postponed until Friday, the 10th inst.

Plucky Rescue at Stockton Heath. During the summer months the Bridgewater Canal at Stockton Heath is much frequented by youthful bathers and happily few serious accidents have to be recorded. On Sunday afternoon, howlver, an exciting rescue was witnessed and a bathing tragedy only narrowly averted by the promptitude and pluck dis- played by George Thomas, the well-known Warrington footballer. About 3.30 in the afternoon two lads were in the water about mid-way between Red-lane Bridge and London Bridge, when one, A. Shepherd (12), 33, Old London-road, got out of his depth. He at once sank and his companion raised an alarm. Thomas, who was fishing close to the spot, was quickly on the scene and only divesting himself of his coat, plunged into the water, succeeding in rescuing Shepherd from the bottom of the canal. Artificial respiration was applied with success and later the lad proceeded home apparently little worse for the accident.

div.head: MARRIAGE' OF MISS PRANCOMB.
div.p: MARRIAGE' OF MISS PRANCOMB.

A pretty and interesting wedding was solemnized at St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, at noon on Wednesday, when Mr. Ernest Charles Griffiths, son of the late Mr. Charles Griffiths, J.P., and of Mrs. Griffiths, of Broken Cross, Northwich, was married to Miss Adeline Maud Francomb, only daughter of Alderman Francomb, J.P., of Wilderspool, Warring- ton, in the presence of a large congregation. The bride, who was given away: by her father, was attired in a charming gown of Irish poplin over an under- dress of white taffeta silk with embroideries of white roses and leaves raised in the material. The bodice was trimmed with real Irish lace, the elbow sleeves being finished with accordion-pleated chiffon. She carried a shower bouquet of white orchids and lillies of the valley, tied with white silk ribbon, and wore a pearl and diamond necklace the gifts of the bride- groom. Her only bridesmaid was Miss Amy Winifred Robinson (daughter of Mr: F. L. Robinson, of Bradford), who was dressed in a pretty gown of white crepe de chine over an underdress of white taffeta, the skirt being trimmed with bands of silk, and the bodice outlined with bands of silk and finished with dainty vest of Valenciennes lace and Irish guipure stole, with which was worn a pale mauve satin sash. Her hat was of white crinoline straw trimmed with tulle and garland of white and mauve lilacs. She carried a bouquet of mauve sweet peas, lilies, and orchids, tied with mauve ribbon, and wore a gold chain bracelet set with rubies and pearls, the gifts of the bridegroom, whose best man was his brother, Mr. Sydney Percival Griffiths. Mrs.Griffiths, mother of the bridegroom wore a beautiful black silk dress relieved with pink roses and black and white 1 crinoline bonnett trimmed with roses to match. The ' Rev. H. A. Lester of St. Thomas's officiated and the service was fully choral. After the ceremony a reception was held at Victoria House Wilders- pool at which owing to the recent bereavement in the bride's family only near relatives were present and later in the afternoon the happy pair left for Colwyn Bay and Holyhead en route for Killarney and the South of Ireland, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling costume consisted of a pale grey cloth coat and skirt, with a bodice of pale grey tucked crepe de chine, the skirt being strapped with the same cloth, and the bolero trimmed with white and pale heliotrope cloth. She wore a black crinoline straw hat trimmed with chiffon and white ostrich feather and a handsome lace scarf —a psesent from the bridegroom's mother, and carried an empire dust cloak of Pale grey silk. Messrs Bollands, of Chester, supplied the wedding cake. The wedding presents were very numerous and of an exceedingly beautiful and costly nature.

div.head: WORKS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WORKS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
The Usefulness of Messrs. Crosflelds' Brigade.

A disastro.us'fire occurred at Warrington on Satur- day at the works of the White Cross Wire Company, Ltd., Bank Quay, Warrington: Tho outVreak was discovered shortly after two o'clock, and the fire brigade of Messrs. Crosfield's were immediately summoned and soon got to work. The large building known as the tinnin,-house, was nell alight and blazing fiercely. A good supply of water was obtained from the works reservoir' and after about an hour's work the men succeeded in getting the fire under,but not before much damage was done. The building was totally wrecked, only the bare walls and a portion of the roof remaining. It is a rather a remarkable circumstance that within the last few days accidents should have occurred in the immediate proximity of both the Liverpoll and the Warrington works of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons Ltd., in both cases to demonstrate the enormous advantage of a private Fire Brigade. •In the former case the fire was observed by one of Crosfield's fire- men to be issuing from a neighbouring cotton ware- house, a bale having caught fire. Without a moment's loss of time he gave the alarm to his own brigade and what would undoubtedly have been a conflagration had been got under before the arrival of the city fire brigade, which owing to later notice and greater distance took some 15 minutes to reach the scene. In the second case, that of Saturday last, when Cros- field's main brigade were able to render such signal service to the neighbouring Whitecross Company, the first tender was out in a few seconds and was immediately followed by the smaller steamer. In fact within less than 3 minutes the whole of the large equipment was away from the station and the firemen engaged in subduing a quick fire which threatened at one time to assume large proportions. Fortunately their steamers were in a position to command the whole of the building involved, and under a com- bined stream of 12,000 gallons per minute all danger was soon at an end. The alarm had not been given at the first outbreak, consequently all that was possible was to save the surrounding buildings. This object was secured, and it is satisfactory to know that the timely intervention of the Brigade localized the effects of the fire. It is due to the officers to say that owing to their practised judgment and careful moderation this was done with the least possible damage to the shell of the building and to the plant, so that repairs can be carried out with a minimum of expense and delay and much resulting unemployment prevented. To Messrs. Crosfield it must be very gratifying that: the new station so soon after its opening has proved ' its value, and that both men and equipment have once more given a practical demonstration of their efficiency. Vurther, the fire, so unfortunate in itself, has at any rate served to show how enlightened is the policy of equipping a brigade with up-to-date time-saving appliances. We are informed that there appears to have been some misunderstanding with regard to the services of the Corporation Brigade. Immediately Supt. Turner heard of the fire he telephoned to ask if the services of the Warrington brigade were required and was told that it was thought Crosfield's Brigade would manage. Sometime later, seeing a large volume of smoke, Supt. Turner again rang up the Whitecross Company, and was told the Warrington Brigade were not wanted. At five minutes to two, however, a cyclist arrived at the station and said the services of the brigade were needed at once. Under Supt. Turner, they turned out with the steam engine " Captain " but when they got there the fire was out.

MUSIC FOR ALL. There are many critics who tell us that our twentieth century life is far too matter-of-fact. They say that in devoting themselves so assiduously to science and invention, we are neglecting to cultivate our finer sus- ceptibilities, and that to redress the balance we need to indulge more frequently in the aesthetic delights which music can afford. , Whether it be true or not that we are pursuing science to the disregard of music, it may ' on the other hand, at any rate, be urged that science is improving the means for the wider dissemination of the delights of music The invention of the talking machine has made it possible for the great mass of the people to enjoy in their own homes the choicest pieces of the price of the better class instruments too high for their moderate purses, but this last difficulty is now removed by the enterprise of the leading firm of talking machine manufacturers, the Columbia Phonograph Company, General. This firm have just put on the market a really high-class instrument which they call the "Jewel " Gmphophone. While possessing all the essential features of the most expensive models, it is sold at the surprisingly low price of four guineas. The Columbia Phonograph Company offer to send full particulars of the "Jewel" Grapktophone to all who write for Leaflet 20 to their European head quarters, 89, Great Eastern-street, London, E.C., and there is little doubt that they will have many enquirers for there are innumerable homes where such an inexpensive means of enjoying the best music will be very much , appreciated.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.
div.p: VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.
THE WEEK'S WORK..

The Warrington volunteers on Saturday departed for their annual camp training on Salisbury Plain where they will join the 13th Field Army Brigade. The Mounted Infantry and Cyclists paraded in the morning and left by an early train whilst the main body of the Battalion to the number of 750 assembled at the Drill Hall at 6.15. Here they were medically examined and all passed as being fit. Colonel Edelsten was in com- mand, and with him were Major J. D. Fairclough,Major F. M. Appleton Major B. Fairclough, Major and Adjutant A. F. Bundock, Captains Layton, C. F. Cary, EL Owen, Patterson, Smith and Williamson, Ridgway! Roberts, Surgeon-Lieutenant Collins, Lieutenants Monks, and Le Page, Second Lieutenants Fairck.ugh and Woods,and Sergeant-Major Ingram. Having paraded in front of the Town Hall, the battalion subsequently marched to the Central Station, headed by the band (under the conductorship of Bandmaster Richardson), which played some popular selections. They marched by way of Sankey-street and Horsemarket-street, which were thickly lined with spectators, and the exception- , ally smart appearance of the men in their khaki uniforms called forth favourable comment. On the arrival at the Central Station the members of the battalion boarded two special trains, which steamed away about half-past seven. The first train, which was under the charge of Colonel Edelsten, conveyed the A, B, C, and D Companies in addition to the band, casuals of the cyclists and Mounted Infantry Companies, whilst the second train was under the charge of Major J. D. Faircloueh and carried E, F, 0, and H and I Companies

div.head: At Windmill Hill. The First Weei's Work.
div.p: At Windmill Hill. The First Weei's Work.

[Br Oust OWN CORRESPONDENT.] The local volunteer battalion—or to give them their full title—the Ist V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment have during the past week been encamped at Windmill Hill, Salisbury Plain. The departure was made at about 8 o'clock on Saturday evening, and despite the heavy downpour of rain, there was a huge crowd of people to give the men a hearty send-off. Pleasing comments were made on the smart appearance of the battalion in the new khaki uniform. On arrival at the station, the troops were quickly entrained in two trains and a start was made. Until it was too dark to see the beautiful scenery in the north of Derbyshire was much admired and then sleep, gentle sleep was predominant through the train. Ludgershall was reached shortly after 4 o'clock on Sunday morning after the quickest run the local soldiers have experienced. The march to camp was quickly accomplished and on arrival there it was found that the camp is almost on the same spot as last year. The only difference is that the doors (?) of the tents are facing due North. This is a great improvement as almost all the wind in this district at this time of the year blows from the South. As usual, the battalion forms part of the 30th Field Army Brigade, in company with the Ist V.B. Royal Welsh Fusiliers, the 2nd V.B. Cheshire Regiment, and the Ist Herefordshire Rifle Volunteers. The last-named did not arrive in camp till Thursday, having marched from Southampton. Sunday was spent in settling down to the new lodgings, and to the issue of boots, shirts, &c. The rain cleared off soon after dinner, and many men left camp for the neighbouring places of interest. There was a very hearty service in the largo marquee belonging to the Y.M.C.A., which does a very good work down here among the troops. It speaks volumes for the Association when it is known that no fewer than 2,106 letters were written and posted in this tent on Sunday only.

WORK COMMENCES.—On Monday morning the men were early astir and going through a round of physical drill under the sergeant-instructors. After breakfast, "fall-in "was sounded at 9.15, and after being photo- graphed on parade, the battalion marched off to area " D "and there took part in some very interesting manceuvres on a small scale. The M. F. company were out skirmishing in the vicinity of Bulford. The signallers, ambulance, and machine gun section were in the vicinity of camp practisinr, in their respective duties. The weather is splendicra good breeze from the south tempering the hot rays of the sun. TUESOXY'S OPERATIONS.—PhysicaI drill was the order of the day in the early morning and after break- fast the battalion went to Area S' C "and got through some good work in general manceveures. The signallers were owt near the camp after dark practising with lamps. OUTPOST DUTY. —On Wednesday morning at 6.30 the battalion were out in the vicinity of camp practising semaphore signalling. There was a very heavy mist and all ranks were glad of the short " double " march which followed. After breakfast, some very interesting movements took place. The battalion marched out of camp in the direction of Ludgershal in the formation of an advanced guard. On reassembling, outposts were thrown out alid a chain of connecting files, &c., formed. , The headquarters were at Lu lgershall and 'Major J. D. Fairclough with the left half battalion was in the woods while the right half battalionunder Major B. Fairclough were stationed on Pitpic Hill. There was no firing, as the idea was simply secrecy of position. The battalion marched back to camp about two o'clock. In the evening, two matches in the first round of the football competion were played. "I " Company gained the mastery over " C " Company while " E " and " F" Companies played a drawn game with a blank sheet. One of "F" Company's players was rather badly hurt.

AN INTERESTING SHAM FIGHT.— At six o'clock on Thursday morning, the mabhine gun section went to the Perham Down range for the annual course of firing. The battalion paraded undar the Adjutant and Com- pany officers at 6.30 for ordinary battalion drill. After breakfast, "A,"" D "and "1 " companies fell in under Captain Crosfleld at 9 o'clock and the rest of the battalion under Major B. Pairclongh paraded a quarter of an hour later, 30 rounds of blank ammunition per man were served out. Area "A " was again allotted to the battalion and the Mounted infantry were given areas "A," " B "and "C." Some very interesting move- ments took place between the rival "armies " during the course ef the morning. Tne general inspection of the battalion will take place to-morrow (Saturday.) The health of the battalion is good and the discipline is well maintainocl only one or two cases of a very minor description being reported.

div.head: SALISBURY SMASH.
div.p: THE SALISBURY SMASH.
Chairman's References at London and
South-Western Meeeting.

Sir Charles Scotter, presiding at the meeting of the London and South-Western Railway Company, on Thursday morning, said there was some melancholy satisfaction in the fact that the cause of the painful accident at Salisbury was not shrouded in mystery. When it was decided to run express trains through Salisbury station, it was distinctly stipulated that the speed should not exceed 30 miles an hour at that point. The working time-table showed this, and every driver on the line was well aware of that limit. Hundreds of trains had been run through that station at that speed without accident. For some reason, unfor- tunately never to be explained now, their train was being driven through Salisbury station at more than 60 miles an hour, and the accident was inevitable. The driver shut off steam after passing the west signal-box, but he omitted to apply his brake. The signalling, the automatic brake on the train, and the permanent way were all perfect, and there was nothing wrong at all except the excessive speed. Sir Charles expressed the great grief of the share- holders and directors at the accident, and their sincere sympathy with the friends and relatives of the victims. , He mentioned that the London and South-Western Railway Company had been remarkably free from acci- dent, and it was the more regrettable that their long record should be now so sadly broken. From the let January, 1889, to the 30th June, 1896, they had carried no fewer than twelve hundred and twenty million passengers or nearly the estimated population of the world, and during that period only one passenger had met his death by accident to the train by which he was travelling. At the conclusion of the meeting Sir Chas. Scotter said he quite agreed with the remarks of a shareholder who thought it was time that racing on railways should cease. So far as that company was concerned, there would he no more racing in future. (Applause).

div.head: EARL'S BROTHER DROWNED.
div.p: EARL'S BROTHER DROWNED.

------ - The Earl of Denbigh has received information that his brother, the Hon. and Very Rev. Monsignor Basil Fielding, was drowned on Tuesday in a boat accident on the Rhine. The body was recovered at Rheinselden,and is being brought to England for interment at Newnham Paddox, near Lutterworth. There arrived at Liverpool on Wednesday from Canada three Red Indian chiefs and a leading tribesman from the Reservations in British Columbia. They have come to this country with the intention of urging King Edward to protect their game reserves.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington now possess a clear lead of one point over Earlestown in the West Lancashire League but it is not due to any success gained on Saturday. They were playing at St. Helens, and after winning the toss the Warrington captain put the home side in with a result that they did not accord with anticipations. S. G. Urruson was one of the first pair and quickly found his form, thirty runs coming from his bat and that of R. Walmsley in a quarter of an hour. After such a good start St. Helens continued to do well and with Urmson making 53. Hammill 39, and Wahusley is, the score reached the good total of 140 for only five wickets before rain came on and closured the proceedings. Warrington would probably have had only a draw to play for, and might possibly have sustained a licking at the hands of the" wooden-spoonists."

The Warrington second eleven at present occupy the head of the second division leatue table though their position) is challenged by Prescot who with two matches in hand are only two points behind the War- rington score. The local eleven have, however, of late been carrying everything before them and if their , present form is maintained they should emerge at the close of the season with flying colours. There only re- mains one league match for them to play and as in this ' they will entertain Prescot on the Arpley ground their leadership should as a result be assured. On Saturday they inflicted a heavy defeat upon the St.Helens second contingent. St. Helens batted first but were unable to do anything with the bowling of Bennett who took six wickets at a cost of five runs each. Dutton's figures were, however, more remarkable as he bowled two balls and captured two wickets.
To the St. Helens total of 66 Warrington replied with 110 for nine wickets. R. G. Pierpoint (23) and R. H. Carson (21) were the principal scorers.

Owing to several of their men being absent at camp Crosfields were able to Send only half a team to meet Moore and Daresbury on Saturday, but they succeeded in making a draw with 60 for 8 wickets as against 92 scored by the home team.

Orford Barracks experienced a shock on Saturday which they will probably feel for some time. They were entertaining the Linotype eleven and succeeded in dismissing them for 78, aby no means big total. The soldiers entered upon their task with confidence, but could do nothing with the bowling of Blease and Kenyon. Davenport with three was the top scorer for the home team whose total only reached 15. Blease took five wickets for five runs, the other four falling to Kenyon.

Mr. "Extras " was the principal scorer in a match between Rylands C.C. and an eleven got together by Mr. G. H. W. Steel. Rylands had first knock and totalled 42. only 30 of which however were scored off the bat. Mr. Steel's eleven replied with 86, out of which 25 was credited to extras. The outstanding feature of the day's play was the bowling of Dilworth, who took seven wickets, four of them with five balls.

Bewsey Wesleyans gave a poor account of themselves on Saturday, scoring ogily 37 in response to a total of 99 for seven wickets ribi up byiArley, The home team had, however, to rely upon the Bros. Smith to give them the victory, as CS of the 99 runs were scored by them, 23 of the balance being the result of lax fielding.

A scratch eleven from Walker's Brewery met Altrincharn St. George's on Saturday, and secured an easy victory, scoring 102 for 7 wickets, as against S 2 For the winners Pearson batted well for his 23, whilst credit is also due to Tichard for his 19 not. out.

Thanks to the bowling of Cox and Conway, Latchford Baptists triumphed with ease over the Penketh eleven. The Baptists batted first and ran up 83, Albinson (20) being the chief scorer. When Penketh took their stand at the wickets their men were rapidly dismissed and their total score did not average two runs a wicket. Cox was practically unplayable four wickets falling to him for one run each. Conway secured three for nine runs.

The flrstof the semi-llnals for the Works Competition drew the largest crowd of the season to the Arpley enclosure on Tuesday evening. Fletchers' and Walkers' Brewery were the opponents and a close struggle was anticipated. Fletcher' had the advantage of first knock but made only poor use of the beautiful wicket and fine . . _ _ _
light. Wood&ick, Thompson. and James hit;rOZ lit out well, but at the close of time only 50 runs had been compiled for the loss of seven wickets.

The Brewery men made light of tho task on coming in to bat and knocked off the runs in 20 minutes. Dargan played particularly well, and made some pretty cuts, while T. Newton treated the crowd to some " clumping " hits until clean bowled by a lob from Williams. In their fifty minutes bAtting, the Brewery men scored 105 runs for the loss of only four wickets, Mogan being not out 41, while Newton had 25 to his credit.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

Further progress was made on Sittirday towards the completion of the Works Competition for the Finlayson Cup, and consolation prizes. One match in connection with the fourth round of the competition proper undecided the victory resting with Fletcher's who had little difficulty in accounting for Sankey Wiro Mills. Practically speaking the match was won and lost in the opening stages as with four men off the '-men Fletchers were in front to the extent of 26 points the ' material and moral value of which could not be over estimated. True Sankey Wire Mills made a fine effort and for a time held their own, but gradually they fell I further behind and in the end retired beaten by 33 points.

The most exciting match in the history of this year's tournament was witnessed in connection with the first round for theconsolltion prizes Longford beating P. and K. (2) by the odd point. To detail the game Sudlow and Ferguson were the first to meet and as a result of Sudlow's good play, Longford acquired a lead of nine points. The game immediately following saw P. and K. come to the front a win of 15-4 in their favour plac- lag them in a good position. A second win further improved their position and ten points separated the teams. This was immediately reduced to almost vanish- ing point by Scott and the fifth game saw Longford again leading, this time by four points.

The match was certainly in an interesting stage and the excitement was increased by the game between Kenwright and Halloway. The P. and E. man at first went to the front and after conceding the lead to Halloway again asserted himself and ran to 10-7. At this point he was over playing his opponent and carried the score to 13-10. P. and K. wanted one point to tie and this was quickly scored by Halloway. A good end saw the score 14-11 and naturally the succeeding end was closely followed, and amid cheers Halloway got a wood homeand gave his side the victory.

The other games in connection with the consolation competition were not productive of much excitement as each was won by a substantial margin. The teams which qualified for the second round were Castle Rubber Co., Rylands (2), P. and K. (3) and Rylands (4).
On account of the holidays no matches will be played this week end but on August 11th play will again be in full swing.

Liberals and Conservatives on SaturdaN. met in friendly opposition on the Liberal Club bowling green, a pleasant afternoon's play resulting in a victory for the Liberals by 41 points. It was on the singles that the advantage was largely gained as in the doubles seven pints only separated the teams. Out of the 27 Igames played the 'Liberals won 17 to their opponents 10.

div.p: Cycling.

Twenty members of the Warrington Cycling Club, tnrned out for the club run to Davenham on Saturday. The weather generally was fine and at the Bully Head Hotel an enjoyable game of bowls was indulged in. On Tuesday there was a good muster for the run to Hoe Green when bowling at the Kilton was again the pro- gramme.

A 'bridegroom once presented the bridesmaids at his wedding with pearl brooches. Judge of his dismay when on reading the account 'of the ceremony, he was informed that the bridesmaids had all worn "handsome [breeches, the gift of the bridegroom."
Ballaghaderin, County Mayo, possesses a population of 1,000 and 72 public-houses. Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman presided on Wednesday at a meeting of the Cabinet. All the Ministers were in attendance.
