div.head: TRIUMPH OF LOVE.
div.p: TRIUMPH OF LOVE.
BY VINCENT WRAY,
Author of "Jacob Gunson, Agitator," "The Folly of His Youth," "Turner's Close," "The Blacksmith's Daughter," &c.

Whilst the majority of British pleasure resorts were desolate and deserted, Llanolwyn still boasted the presence of visitors. Not many, of course, for it was the month of December, and Christmas was near at hand. But the picturesque Welsh watering-place has special attractions during the winter season. Not, be it understood, in the shape of concerts, balls, pitntomimes, and the like, but owing solely to the gentleness of its climate. The big masses of mountain that hem it in on the, east—that, in fact, may almost be said to hold it in fond and warm embrace—shut out the cold, piercing, inhospitable winds which are so terribly trying to the weak and ailing. Even the waters of the bay which, on the west, sweep round in a glorious curve, are rarely troubled by the fierce gales which now and again, and with lamentable frequency, lash into un- governable fury the more exposed parts of the Atlantic. Thus does it happen that some folks who can afford to do it "winter" at Llanolwyn; and they contentedly declare that the experience is quite as delightful as—of course, much less costly—a sojourn 'neath the sunny skies and amidst the balmy breezes of Mentone. Generally speaking, the visitors "put up" at the elaborate hotels which enterprise has pro- vided. Private apartments are never popular during the winter months. This the Llanolwyn landlady knows full well, and, accordingly, reckons to make her year's keep in the season. If by chance, or good fortune, she encounters a stranger who prefers "home comforts" and free- dom to the somewhat systematised and restricted routine of hotel life, she immediately shakes hands with herbelf, and prepares to receive the envious congratulations of her friends and neighbours. In the particular December to which this story has reference, Mrs. Llewelyn Jones was the landlady upon whom "good luck" had smiled. On the third of the month a young lady called upon her. She gave her name as Miss Violet Carpenter' and expressed the intention of taking apartments in Llanolwyn. Mrs. Llewelyn Jones —it is necessary to repeat the "Llewelyn" to distinguish her from the many other Joneses in the town—smilingly professed her willingness t.; oblige. The rooms at liberty were shewn and approved, and, better than all references, a fortnight's rent was paid down "on the nail." Mrs. Llewelyn Jones at once manifested con- siderable interest in her new lodger, and not without excellent reason. Violet Carpenter could boast of a great deal more than the ordinary share of good looks. Fair, tall, and undeniably graceful, she presented a striking 'example of English beauty. Added to this, her every word and gesture denoted high breeding and culture. "A perfect lady," decided Mrs. Llewelyn'Jones, who was no mean judge of such matters; and the worthy woman straightway began to wonder by what concourse of circum- stances her visitor had been driven, or induced, whichever it might be, to come alone, at this season of the year,to Llanolwyn. For the present, at any rate, Mrs. Llewelyn Jones's curiosity had to feed upon those endless surmises of which the creative brain of the average landlady is capable. Carefully-veiled inquiries, gentle hints, diplo- matically suggested, alike were futile. Miss Carpenter obstinately refused to be "drawn." Never by so little as a stray word did she give any clue to her home, her friends, or the reason of her visit to the little Welsh town. "She's young, but you may depend upon it that she's got a history," was the conclusion at which Mrs. Llewelyn Jones eventually arrived, though, unlike many of her class, she had the good sense te keep her opinion to herself. The first week of Violet's stay at Llanolwyn was uneventful. She passed most of her time by the seashore. A favourite seat of hers was a big, rough boulder against which, at high water, playful wavelets rolled, to be broken into slender columns of spray. Here the girl would sit for hours at a stretch, gazing wistfully out upon the wide waste of waters. She was lonely, and in the loneliness of the sea she seemed to find the sympathy she longed for. Violet Carpenter was miserable and heartbroken, and it was true that she had a history. But what that history was, how terrible and tragic in the events it comprised, not even Mrs. Llewelyn Jones cbuld have imagined. She had loved tenderly and devotedly, and she still loved. Her very presence at Llanolwyn was an indication of the depth, the sincerity, the unselfishness of her passion. It was the evening of the second day of the *cond week of her stay in Llanolwyn. She sat in her accustomed place watching the heaving bosom of ocean and thinking over the troubled events of her life. One man was the world to her. Again and again had she listened to his -strong pleadings to his fervent vows, to his declarations of eternal fidelity. And now-- "Cyril, I can die for you!" she cried. "And I will—l will. But, oh! that it could have been otherwise. Why is it that Fate is so cruel, so unfeeling?" She sobbed bitterly, and the moaning of the sea blended with the anguish in her voice. The tide was coming in; already the water was creeping around the base of the rock. Even now she could not return without wetting her feet, but she did not seem to notice it. Grief is as absorbing as joy. Neither did she hear the sound of footsteps behind her. A voice, with an unmistakable foreign accent, called her name.

"Violet, I have found you!" The girl started like a guilty thing. Then she sprang from her seat, splashed through the shallow water, and faced the speaker. "Antonio Sanzio—you!" she exclaimed. "Yes," he returned, with a low chuckle. "A pleasant surprise for you, no doubt." "How did you find me? Why did you follow me here?" she gasped. "How did I find you? Why did I follow you?" he repeated. "These questions, sweet one, are as erity to answer as they are to ask. As for the first, you of all people should know that the movements of so celebrated, so gifted, so charming a young woman as Violet Carpenter, the actresa, are not difficult to trace. Do you really want me to reply to the second question, to repeat the story I told you two years ago, before *he cold-blooded Englishman came between us with his false vows end falser heart ?"
"No. no, no, you wrong him, Antonio. He is not false-hearted. If the force ,of eircum- stances--" _

"Bah!" The Italian made a gesture of contempt. "What is the force of circumstances when pitted against the power of love? Do you think / would have allowed anything,any circum- stances, to have parted us ? " The man spoke English fluently, and with the natural eloquence of his race. "I tell you,' he went on, without pausing for a reply, "Cyril Henshaw is a coward and a traitor; he is unworthy of a passing 0,,5 from you the memory of th

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 4, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 4, 1906.

calcinating, unfeeling English m a n ; crush it under foot as you would a thing vile, loathsome, dis- tasteful. Whatever has happened, I love you. Yes, I swear it. I love you, and—" "Oh, hush!" exclaimed Violet, alarmed by the man's terrible earnestness and impassioned pleading, "you must not talk to me like this. You do not know all, you cannot know, or—or you would not say all this to me." "And still you repulse me—for this English- man ? "

"Yes—yes. I—" "Then, listen." There was a marked change in Antonio's voice. His words came hissing through clenched teeth, and the foreign accent grew more pronounced. "Antonio Sanzio truly loves but once. His passion is deathless as his soul. I love you—you only, do you hear me? am an Italian, and our race know well how to avenge treachery towards the women of their choice. I will seek out Cyril Henshaw, and I will kill him. Kill him, do you understand? Kill him as ruthlessly as I would a dog or a rat, or the snake that strikes from its hiding-place. By all I hold sacred, I swear that the scoundrel shall die! It is now the eleventh of December. There are yet thirteen days to Christmas. Thirteen days of life for Cyril' Henshaw. What do you say to a Christmas Eve tragedy? Look at this • look at it, do you hear me F" Violet caught a glimpse of cold, glittering steel. "No, no," she cried; "you do not under- stand. You--"
"Yes, I understand too well," he retorted, savagely; "and I swear that this shall bury itself hi his treacherous heart, and avenge your wrongs."

"But believe me," she implored, "he has not wronged me. I had not intended telling you, but, indeed, before Heaven and -earth, in the sight of God and man, I am his lawful wife!" "Ah! to save him you lie; and you lie in vain. I have spoken, and I will fulfil my vow." "No, no! Come back, Antonio! Oh, come back!"

The words might as well have been hurled at the unheeding ocean. Already the Italian's form was receding into the gathering shadows; and the moan of the sea answered the pitifulness of her weary heart. "Cyril,. my love," she gasped, "my sacrifice shall not be vain. You are in danger; he is so fierce, or wild, so unforgiving. You shall be warned. I will save you from him, even though it be for another woman." 11.

The Hon. Cyril Henshaw, eldest son of the Marl of Linden, and heir prospective to the title, was engaged in anxious conference with George D. Prance, the Yankee timber king. The two men were in the library of Belmont House, London. The subject they were discussing was momentous enough in all conscience. The Hon. Cyril was in sore need of money; the plebeian, Prance was every bit as desirous of obtaining the tide for his daughter. It was a matter of mutual advantage, and the arrangement was now being definitely settled. There was not even a semblance of romance. , Maria Prance was perfectly willing to becomb Lady Linden, and her father was just as ready to hand over the dollars that would pay off the heavy mortgages which encumbered the estates.. •

"It's now December 23rd," said Prance, with a Yankee drawl. ."On the 26th, we'll have a splash-up wedding, and, as the money's all safe and sound, you can spend your Christmas Day. in peace." "Is there any peace for the wicked ?" said Cyril, with a tinge/of sadness that was lost upon the man of millions. "Well, I'm inclined to think that the wicked- ness doesn't so much matter so long as there's brass enough to cover it. It isn't what a man is, but what a man has that makes him go through the world smiling. Now, the Hon. Cyril Henshaw can boast a long and honourable line of ancestors, but unfortunately one's forefathers can't hand down bank-notes from their coffins, and without bank-notes it's not very much use being the son of a belted Earl." "True enough," returned the young aristocrat, and he very nearly added, "as I know to my cost," only it suddenly struck him that even in an affair of hard cash like this such a sentiment must appear ungallant and ill-advised. "Now to business," said Prance. "On the day that Maria becomes your wife, the future Countess of Linden "—he lingered affectionately on the title—"l shall hand you a cheque for one hundred thousand pounds, with a father's blessing." "Bother the blessing!" mutteNd Henshaw, in an aside as the image of Maria Prance seemed to rise before him. He had not seen much of her, but quite sufficient.. She was tall, cgarse, unshapely, and, what the Hon. Cyril detested most of all, had red hair. She spoke in a low, rasping, imperious voice: and he knew well enough that, when the ceremony was over, Maria Prance was not likely to fofget the part her father's money had played in the transaction. Then, too, there Via s a anemory of the past which haunted him, a face exquisitely tender and beautiful that was indelibly pictured in the tablets of his heart—the gentle, .self-sacrificing; noble-hearted Violet Carpenter, whom he was ruthlessly sacrificing for g01d.," All this, and much more of a similar kind, flashed through his mind with the speed that belongs to thought, when the cold, matter-of-fact voice of the American reminded him of the business they were discussing. "Listen here, Henshaw," he said, "I don't know why you want to drop down into these gloomy fits. One would think that we were dis- cussing your funeral instead of your marriage with a beautiful bride, whose father is going to come down handsomely." "I thought we agreed," retorted the younger man, "that the affair, is to be considered strictly one of convenience. 'I want the money, you want the 'tide for your daughter ; and I tell you plainly that, when the marriage is over, so far as I am concerned, the future Countess of Linden" —he laid ironical stress on the title—"can go back again across the Atlantic, and leave her husband to enjoy the paradoxical condition of being a married bachelor." "Oh, of course," replied the millionaire. "We've had all that over before, but, you know, it's part of the contract that my Maria shall live tip to her station and take her place in society." "If Maria doesn't mind," suggested Henshaw, with a significant shrug of his shoulders, "I'm prepared to endure her. ' "Oh, Maria doesn't mind," said Prance—"not in the least. She's a good girl, only a bit ambitious, and I'm sure that, with the education she's had, she'll not discredit even the noble name and house of the Earls of Linden." All this, of course, was distasteful to the Hon. Cyril, and again is sweet face full of unuttered reproach and devotion passed before him. "I am not quite sure—" he began, when he was inteirupted by a knock at the door. A servant handed him a letter. He glanced at the hand- writing on the envelope, and then, with a courteous, "Pardon me, please!" tore it open. This is what he read: "Am waiting at the end nf the road. Please see me. This is imperative and urgent. Your very life depends on your complying. —VIOLET." For a moment dazed, he stared at the missive and mechanically read it again. Then his face paled. He crumpled up the note and thrust it into one of his pockets. "Bad news, eh? " said Prance, inquisitively. "No, no, no," returned Henshaw; "that is--" "Well," interrupted the millionaire, "Maria's waiting to speak to her future husband. Believe me my girl will get devoted to you if you'll only let her." "Hang Maria!" retorted Henshaw; then added quickly: "Of course, I "didn't mean that, but— but--well, I hardly know what I do mean, only I think we had better finish this business at some other time."

And he abruptly left the room. - "Well, this is a go!" exclaimed the million- aire. "I never knew anything lie these young aristocrats: They don't seem to know when they've got a good thing on. Here's 'Maria and one hundred thousand pounds, and yet he don't seem anxious to close the bargain. Ah, well, a few hours'll make no difference, and George D. Pfance can rest assured now that he's hooked an Earl for his Maria."

"To warn you—to put you on your gua:::!,'• was the reply. "You are in danger, Cyril; in greater danger than you can imagine. The Italian has turned up, and he vows that—" "That he will be avenged on me, and all the rest of it," put in Henshaw. "I know the style of swaggering braggadocio. Bahl They're all alike, these hot-blooded, self-opinionated foreigners." "B—but do be watchful, Cyril; don't treat the affair too lightly," pleaded Violet. "I know full we that Antonio means mischief. He told me hellhould seek you out and would kill you." "Very obliging and considerate of him, I'm sure. Thanks for your kindly warning. I presume there is no ulterior motive in your plan for arranging this interview ? " A rich crimson colour surged into the woman's. fair cheeks, and her voice trembled as she replied. "No—of course not. Only—" "Only what ? " "Tell me, Cyril, cannot this thing be pre- vented? Must it go on ? " What, the marriage? Yes, I auppose " The young fellow's face clouded and a frown settled on his brow. "You know as well as I do that I'm personally over head and ears in. debt, and my father's estates are as heavily encumbered as they can possibly be. Of course, I know well enough that you Can put a stop to it any minute. One word from you, and---" "I have a confession to make, Cyril." "Then get on with it. I suppose it's nothing very serious.l 'Oh, yes it is. Antonio swore that you had betrayed me,and, to save you from his vengeance, told him the truth."

"You—you told him the truth—that you are my wife!" exclaimed Henshaw. "Then I am ruined—absolutely ruined." "But, Cyril,, think. Your second marriage would not have been legal. You would have brought yourself within the grasp of the criminal law. Perhaps it might never have been found out, and yet—" • "Well ? " he exclaimed, fiercely. "Do you think you could be happy with—with the lady, Cyril ?, ' "Happy ? No! It is for gold—for gold, that hard, glittering, cruel thing for which men sell thPir lives, their souls, their honour." "Listen!" Her voice sank to a whisper. "We were married, you and I, quietly, in an out-of- the-world kind of place. You took an assumed name; I consented to keep the affair secret. Then your love grew cool, the flame of your passion went out. You explained your cares to me; told me how you were placed; how, unless I agreed to eternal separation ruin stared you in the face. In an evil moment I let you have your way. I cannot now understand why L fell in with your suggestions. The only excuse I can offer is that I loved you, and that woman's love is wholly unselfish and devoted. At any rate, I gave up the triumph of the stage, the ambition of my life, and dropped out of public view. I promised to look on, whilst you, spurning my love, perjured yourself at God's holy altar. Now I have come to warn you. There is peril before you. Antonio will find you out, he may learn the truth, and then nothing could save 3:" _
She paused, but Henshaw spoke not. "One thing more I can do for you—only one thing more. When are you to be married ? "On the 26th," Henshaw replied, mechanically.
~ .. . "You need have no fear then, so long as you can avoid Antonio's vengeance. By the 26th you will be free—free to marry the gold which is more to you than all the world besides."

It was the evening before the day fixed for the wedding. The millionaire was jubilant; his daughter was in equally high spirits. Cryil Henshaw alone was miserable. He paced the floor of the library of Belmont House with im- patient strides. "You will be free, you will be free." He kept repeating the significant words Violet Carpenter had used. What did they mean? What terrible happening did they suggest? Surely not— He dared' not give utterance to the thought that now for the first time flashed into his brain. If Violet Carpenter nobly went to her death, he—he--Cyril Henshaw, the last of an honoured race, would be her murderer. "And she loves me—loves me as this wretched Prance girl never could love." He gave utterance to the sentiment that forced itself upon him. "I must go out—out into the air, or I shall go mad." He let himself out quietly. The street was deserted, save for an organ-grinder who seemed to be wending his way home. Henshaw noticed him, and threw him a shilling. Had he cared to watch the man' he would have seen him spurn the coin with his foot, and trample it into the mire. The Earl's son wandered on, his gloomy thoughts chilling his blood, and whispering fearful accusations into his heart. "Murderer, murderer," said the voice; "murderer and blackguard !", He was shadowed; but he was too distracted to observe it. At a distance, but keeping Henshaw well in view, followed the organ- grinder. Henshaw wandered on and on, heedless alike of time and place. Suddenly, he paused. He had come into one of the largest quarters of the city, and was standing near the gateway of a church. The door was open, and he entered. There were many people there, but in silent • prayer. He, too, knelt down; he also prayed. The organ-grinder silently followed, his fierce eyes fixed upon Henshaw. The sanctuary had a soothing effect upon Cyril's troubled mind. He could not explain it; but a strong influence seemed to seize hold of him. Yet there was nothing to attract the eye • no music to soothe the troubled breast. The lights shone dimly upon the altar; the massive stonework looked hard and bare and unsympathetic. With Henshaw's prayer came a new resolve, a new hope. The organ-grinder, too, was deeply moved. The sight of the proud Englishman, bowed in the attitude of prayer, touched his hn- pressianable nature. He was a devout Catholic, and he could not resist the peaceful influence of the place. He trembled violently, and then, making the sign of the Cross, he muttered: "My vengeance must die. He will do right by her. Oh, altar of Christ! Oh, Cross of Christ, thou hast conquered ! " It was fully an hour before Henshaw left the building. The organ-grinder followed. "Cyril Henshaw," he said, putting a hand .on his shoulder, "you will do right by)ter. Promise me."
Strange to say, Henshaw evinced no surprise. 41 Where can I find her?" he asked, quietly. "At Llanolwyn," was the reply.

. . - . . . "Thank Heaven that I did not come too late." For Cyril Henshaw only reached the little Welsh watering-place in time to avert a tragedy. "Why have you come ? " asked Violet. "What has made you seek me out ? " "It is the triumph of love," answered Cyril; "the triumph of love over So, too, in the case or Antonio Sanzio. It vas the triumph of love—but love of another and nobler kind. - .
[THE END.)
"Violet! "

"Cyril !" To the outward observer there was nothing extraordinary in the exchange of greeting. Not- ivithstanding the use of the Christian names, either inight only have been a somewhat distant acquaintance of the other. There was a kind of coldness, of reserve, a sort of standoflishness which might have been taken to indieste the existence of strained relationship. Certainly there was no evidence of affection..

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR. At the Borough Police Court on Monday. before the Mayor and other justices, George Farrell, 24, Padgate- lane, applied for a certificate exempting his child from vaccination.—The Mayor : Have you a conscientious objection ?—Applicant : Yes.—The Mayor : What do you call a conscientious objection ?—Applicant : I believe vaccination will be detrimental to the health of the child.—The Mayor : Bow do you arrive at that idea ? —Applicant : Nature makes a healthy child.—Mr. W. Roberts: Have you had any previous experience ? —Applicant : This is my first child. Mr. Thornton : If he states that he has a conscientious objection that is enough.—The Mayor : If that is the law the applica- tian is granted. VACCINATION EXEMPTION REFUSED. Charles Whitehead applied before the Warrington magistrates on Wednesday, for a vaccination exemption order, but was unable to convince the chairman (Mr. Charles White)of the necessity of granting it. Applicant stated that he bad a conscientious objection,hecause one of his children died:from the effects:of vacclnation.—The Chairman.: It never has that is not true. No one dies from yucination.—Applicant : Well, it was from/the effects.—The Chairman : You will have to come another day. I have a conscientious objection to signing the order. Supposing the child were to catch smallpox and die, would you not be guilty of murder ?—Applicant : No sir.—The application was refused. THEFT AT PENKETII. Thomas Branev, labourer, Penketh, pleaded guilty, nt the Warrington County Sessions on Wednpsday to steal- ing ss. from the till of the Crown Tnn,Penketh. It was stated that. prisoner xvert into the inn on Monday after- noon, ordered some liquor, but, having no money, was unable to pay for it. Whilst the landlord's wife, Mrs. Johnson,was away in the kitchen the prisoner helped him- self to the contents of the till. The magistrates im- posed a fine of 20s. and costs, or fourteen days.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.

CHLOROFORM FOR WHOOPING COUGH. Dr. Henri de Rothschild, the wealthy French Baron, has discovered that chloroform will cure whooping cough. A child suffering from hip disease and whooping cough at the same time was in his hospital, and the youngster was put under an anesthetic while an operation was per- formed. It was noticed that on regaining con- sciousness the cough had decreased. It occurred to the doctor to try chloroform as a cure for the cough. He found that it worked admirably, effecting a speedy recovery.

FINSEN LIGHT FOR HEART DISEASES. Dr. Hasselbach, of Copenhagen, has become convinced that the Finsen light treatment is effective in heart disease and affections of the nervous system. After experimenting on his own perfectly normal organs, he next experimented on two medical men. Both of these were com- plete invalids, one suffering from angina pec- toris (heart affection), and the other from a ner- vous affection of the heart. This treatment, which lasted in one case for a month, and in the other for six weeks, resulted in enabling both doctors to resume their practice.

div.head: SOLID MOUNTAIN OF IRON.
div.p: A SOLID MOUNTAIN OF IRON.

A mountain which is said to be the most re- markable in the world is situated in the State of , Durango, Mexico. It certainly has a claim to this reputation, for it is 2,000 ft. high, about ' three-quarters of a mile in thickness at the base. , and is almost solid iron. Naturally, it has been the dream, ever since its discovery, of iron manufacturars, to lease the mountain and work it. But this tho Mexican Government has re- fused to let them do until quite recently. The ore obtained from this mountain is said to yield , about 87 per cent. pure iron.
\ - PROGRESS OF THE TECHNOLEXICON.

Dr. Hubert Jansen reports that the great technical dictionary undertaken by the Society of German Engineers, upon the compilation of which in three languages—English, German, and French—some 2,000 firms and individual colla- borators are engaged, has now so far advanced towards completion that printing will begin early in 1907. The work will be issued by Messrs. J. J. Weber, Illustrierte Zeitung office, Leipsic. Some idea of the scope of this dic- tionary may be obtained from the fact that over 3,000,000 word-cards have been collected. Dr. Jansen's editorial address is Dorotheenstrasse 49, Berlin (NW. 7.).

EARTHQUAKES AND TALL CHIMNEYS. One of the lessons to be learnt from the easthquake in San Francisco appears to be that the ordinary tall brick chimney is a great source of danger when earth movements take place, par- ticularly when the chimneys are built with large heavy caps. Of course, where tall stacks are constructed of reinforced concrete the case is different, as also it is with comparatively short steel stacks. It would therefore appear that, in countries subject to earthquake shocks, it would be a wise precaution to build chimneys either of reinforced concrete if tall, or of. steel •if low, and use mechanical draught with the latter. If brick alone be used, the chimneys should be built short, and not have heavy caps.

div.head: USEFUL ALLOY.
div.p: A USEFUL ALLOY.

Acootding to the Iron Age, two parts of alu- minium and one part of zinc form an alloy eo which the name cif " algene " has been given. The strength of this alloy is equal to good cast iron, and is superior to it so far as the elastic limit is concerned. It does not easily oxidise, and takes a fine polish. It melts at a low red-beat and becomes very fluid, and it will then fill small thin places. While melting it, great care must be exercised, 'Particularly when mixing the two metals. The alloy is not suited for articles which require the toughness possessed by bars. but there are many purposes for which it can be used with advantage. It has a tensile strength of about 22,0901 b. per square inch, and its swats gravity is 31.

div.head: REPORTED NEW ELEMENT.
div.p: REPORTED NEW ELEMENT.

According to a Cologne paper, Professor Bat. telli, of the University of Pisa, has discovered a new element more powerful even in its action than radium. He observed some time ago in the water of the San Giuliano spring some re- markable shining 6ppears,nces, and alter many sx-teriments be found these waters to be strongiv radio-active. He accordingly set to work to col- lect and condense the gaseous emanation's, and installed steam-pumping machinery for this pur- pose. The gas procured by these means was. after being purified, conducted by small tubes coated with zinc sulphide into liquid air. The condensed gas at once became apparent, and imparted a green colour to the sulphur. No de- terrniza.:ion respecting the nature of this sub- stance has, however, yet been possible.
NON-FERRUGINOTiS MAGNETIC ALLOYS.

Furthet experiments on the magnetic proper- ties exhibited by ton-ferruginous alloys are de- scribed by A. Gray in the proceedings of the Royal Society, 1906. A rod of copper alloyed with 16 per cent. of manganese, 8 per cent, of aluminium, and a trace of lead was found to be almost non-magnetic, but after heating at 340 deg. C. for a short ,time its magnetic proper- ties increased considerably. Further heating at 400 deg. C. followed by immersion in cold water removed the magnetic quality, the critical tem- perature at which the change Was effected being 350 deg. At the temperature of liquid air the de- magnetised alloy was again found to be sus- ceptible to magnetic influence, although retain- ing its magnetism less than when heated at 340 deg. Manganese appears to be the essentia/ constituent of these non-ferruginous compounds

div.head: IF WATER NEVER FROZE.
div.p: IF WATER NEVER FROZE.

snow and ice, with all the results flowing from these phenomena, would vanish. With the dis- appearance of glaciers, the regular supply 'of water to our largest rivers would fail, end their volume be so modified as to amount to a redis- tribution of the fresh water of the globe. Moun, taineering without the avalanche and glacier would be robbed of itei chief danger, excitement, and, to some minds, its main attraction. The Arctic Seas, cleared of icebergs and floes, would be rid of the greatest obstacles at present Offered to navigators, and would offer an easy passage to either pole. The moisture disintegrating power exerted by rain and moisture becoming frozen after they have entered fissures and cre- vices of rock would cease to act, and the trees- porting agency of icebergs, which have been .in- strumental in forming submarine banks like those of Newfoundland, would come to an end.

BEETLE THAT BORED THROUGH LEAD. In the Journal of the Society of Chemical In- dustry, Mr. William B. Hart describes a case in which a wood-boring insect was,found capable of making its way through a sheet of lead kin. thick. The insect in question was the giant wood wasp Sirex gigas. The sheet of lead per- forated by the insect was intended for the straps of a lead sulphuric chamber, and had been laid tmporarily on a wooden floor, and this in turn on wooden joists. The insect came from one of the latter, in which it had grown to maturity, and then endeavoured to make its escape by bor- inr, up through the floor and the leaden plate above the latter. The time taken certainly did not exceed forty-eight hours, as the leaden plate had only been in position for that length of time. In 4 few hours more the insect would certainly have escaped, being steadily at work at the time it was detected.

div.head: SENSE OF COLOUR IN ANIMALS.
div.p: THE SENSE OF COLOUR IN ANIMALS.

The hypothesis that the sense of colours is pos- sestied to a high degree by animals, and espe- cially by birds, furnished a basis for some of the most beautiful and fecund of the Darwinian theories of sexual selection. No Darwinist doubts that the brilliant colours of the male birds of some species are destined to attract the atten- tion of the female birds, and this presupposes naturally on the part of these birds a fine sense of colour. Wallace has asserted that to the fact that certain plants bear fruit of brilliant colours is due their preservation; the animals, at- tracted by these colours, break the fruits from the trees or plants, carry them off, and thus indirectly assist in the dissemination of the seeds which they contain over latge tracts of land. And this function of selection on the part of animals presupposes in them a certain sense of colour. Still, scientific documents in support of these hypotheses are rare. Dahl, alluding to the scarcity of them in an article in the Naturwis- aenachaftliche Wochenschrift, relates some in- teresting experiments which he made with a monkey. He coloured some sweets with a cer- tain coloured dye, and some bitter substances with that of' another colour, and declares that after a few attempts, the monkey learnt to leave without even tasting those articles of food coloured with the dye which indicated bitter- tasting cubstances, and seized at once upon those which indicated sweets. Varying the experi- ments sufficiently. he found that the monkey diatimmished all the different colours readily. save only dark blue. Valli calls attention to the fact that Mayer has stated that many c..avage tribes cannot distingiush dark blue from black, and that even children do not distinguish this 'Dieu until later than all others.

div.head: DOG AND THE: TEACUP.
div.p: THE DOG AND THE: TEACUP.

There was once a dog—Oh, such a very big dog—which looked so savage and ill-natured that strangers crossed over to the other side of the road when they saw him coming. And yet this dog—that was not to be cowed by man or woman, or boy or girl, or anything living—was afraid of a teacup! Yes, Nero, the large wolf- hound, was afraid of a teacup; and I will tell you why. One day Nero was poorly. His eyes were dull and heavy, his nose was hot and dry, and his tongue was parched; and when all these things happen to a dog, you may be sure he is not well. So Nero's master sent for the dog-doctor. Dog-doctor Jones came. Nero was very cross, for he did not like to be stared at, and hummed at, so he barked a good deal; and Dr. Jones did not like the sound of that bark any more than he liked the look of Nero gener- ally. "Humph," said the doctor to himself; and, after scratchivg his head to make him think better, home he went, trotting, on his fat old cob; and half-an-hour later he sent some- thing in a bottle for Nero. When Nero's master took the cork out of the bottle, he said, "Phewl my dog won't like this." Se he poured the physic into a small teacup, and 'walking up to the kennel, called "Nero." Nero tried to wag his tail; but tails are hard things to switch round when a dog feels poorly, so Nero's tail gave only a tiny bit of a waggle, and then dropped straight. "Poor old fellow," said his master; "you will not like this medicine, I fear, but it will make you well." Then, placing his fingers at the back of Nero's jaws., he opened his mouth; and, while Nero's mouth was open, "pop" went the physic down the dog's throat. Nero sneezed and sneezed, and curled his nose into all kinds of queer puckers. He would have been angry tad he not been ill. But I am glad to tell you that one dose cured him. Now, when John wants to sweep the yards, and Nero objects—trying hard to worry the brush—John just slips into the kitchen, gets a teacup, and shows it to Nero. Nothing more is,needed to subdue his warlike spirit. Off he runs into his kennel, crouching and trembling with fear—just fancy, at the sight of a teacup I—l remain, your loving Nephew,
JOHN JAMES DTJMELOW.

div.head: GENTLE WORDS.
div.p: GENTLE WORDS.

Use gentle words, for who can. tell The blessings they impart./ How oft they fall (as manna fell) Upon some fainting heart. In lonely ,wilds by light-winged bird, Rare seed's have oft been sown, And hope has sprung from gentle words, Where only grief had grown. From, Liz= WILLS.

div.head: MUCH-NEEDED LESSON.'
div.p: A MUCH-NEEDED LESSON.'
A certain German duke hit upon a novel plan for teaching hde neighbours diligence. In the

night-time, when no-one was about, he: placed a great stone in the centre of a road near his palace. In the early morning a heavy waggon came lumbering along, driven by a sturdy peasant. 'What a shame to leave this big stone right in the middle of the way," said the peasant. But, though disgusted at the laziness of other people, he made no attempilbto move the stone himself. He guided his steeds past I it with care, and then proceeded on his way: I The next to pass that way was a man on horse- back. The animal shied at the obstacle in the road, and nearly threw his rider, who stormed at the abominable way these country roads were kept. But. he, too, passed on his way with- out making an effort to remove the stone and prevent another suffering the eame mischance that had so nearly befallen him. A soldier lot- lowed the horseman. He was whistling a gay air, and paid n.o heed to where he wats going. As a result, he did not see •the stone, but stumbled over it, measuring his length, on the road. His indignation was great, and he used not a few hard words in speaking of the people of the district, and he also continued his way grumbling. All sorts and conditions of people passed that. way during the. next week or two, but not one took the trouble to move the stone from the road, and at the end of a month it still lay in the same spot, a source of danger to the unwary. Then the duke caused it to be made known that he desired all his neighbours to meet him, at that spot at a certain. hour. Curious as to the duke's motive, a crowd assembled, and were thus addressed by the duke:—" My friends, four weeks ago I placed this stone here. People in plenty have, passed this way during that time, but the, stone still lies in the same position. No one has troubled to move, it, though all have grumbled at his neighbours for not taking it away." Having delivered this little speech, the duke lifted the stone and exposed to view a small bag, which lay snugly beneath it. The bag bore the in- scription :—" For him who lifts the stone," and untying the. string that fastened it, the duke took out a beautiful ring, and twenty golden coins. I leave you to picture the surprise and disappointment of the onlookers. Any one of them 'might have become the owner of these treasures had he but taken the: pains to move the titone, instead! of walking round it and leav- ing the task for someone else, Let us hope they benefited by the lesson taught them by the duke. LIZZIE WILLS.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to tell you how well my garden is doing. All ray plants are flowering, except the sunflowers. I hope to enjoy my holidays. On Saturday I went to Matlock, being a Juvenile Oddfellow. I en- joyed myself very much. I enjoyed the ride on the switch-back immensely. The train did not start back till 9.25, and it got back in Burton about 10.20. I am sending you a short piece of poetry. I hope you will like it.
From your loving Nephew, HAROLD CHAMBERLAIN.
MISCHIEF.

Round about the pantry, Up and down the shelf, Seizing wliat he fancies, Trips a naughty elf. Nibbles at the bacon, Tastes a bit of meat; Finds the butter handy, Tarts so good to eat. Tasting all the dainties, Has a lovely meal; Thinks he's very lucky, Never means to steal. But when cook is coming, Runs into his house, For this little robber Is a tiny mouse 1

Dear Uncle Ned,—l was very, very glad to see my name in print. I am sending you two very nice -pieces of poetry, which I hope you will like. I would very much like to see one of these in 'print. I hope you and all the circle are well. I have not got any more to say this time, so I will close my letter.—l remain, your loving friend, MILLIE SMITH. THE GOLDEN RULE. div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE HOLIDAY MONTH.

August is the holieay month, even more in Free Church circles than in the general business world. The reg War Free Church minister's holiday is a month, and it usually is August. Most Free Church ministers, therefore, are sup- posed to be away at the seaside or in the colmtty. Of Course there must be exceptions, for all ttirou;lh the month the work of open-air services will he carrie,l on vigorously. There is no reason at all why Church services should not be held more and more oat of doors during these Weeks. Several CixorcLes have made the inno- vation recei,tl,y of_l!,)ldiug their regular s:rvices

out of church. a:-“1 this is a. custom "w 1 nch might surely in many p!acc,s l'e adopted. Free Church Councils, at any rate, seem to have postponed indoor meetings for a few weeks, and garden par i ies and oT.en-air domo.nstrat ions are quite the rule. , This makes a ,ttuit variety, and is 'practically always successitexcept when it rains.

div.head: lIARIZOGATS CONVENTION.
div.p: THE lIARIZOGATS CONVENTION.

The chief Free Church event of the month will he the Convention at Harro,Fatte d ming the week ctimmencinz, August 12. Inis Convention will be on slightly new lines to those' held during the summ,:r months of recc nt years.. It .isto be a sort of P:oe Church Keswici:. NO re- presiMtatives v.-ill be appointed from local Councils, and no 'hospitality Wli he , provided- A it of hotels, &c., of en to ail,T.rd accommo. dstion Ins I.ecn 1-mpared. and win be sent on rent hy the Rev.. Themr:: Law, Muporial Hall, 'London, E.C. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., will he in charge of the meetings, and will preach in the Baptist Church on Sundays, August 12. and 19t On Monday evening there Will be a Welcome Mod in .2, at 7.80. On Tues- day, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday the order of meetings will he as follows At 7.30 a.m. a start will 'be made With a Sunrise Prayer Meeting; at e,even o'clock theie Will' be a Con- ference-oi direct devotional lines. In the after- noon the members of the Convention will assemble for a ramble to the places of interest in' the neighbourhood.' At five o'clock a public tea \ will be served, and the opportunity will be taken of a short talk on various departments of Free Church- work. All these meetings will take place at the Baptist Church, but the even- ing gatherings at 7.80 will be held in the Wesleyan Church, and will be of an evan- gelistic character. Among. those taking par in the meetings are, in addition to Mr. Meyer, Dr. Horton, Rev. Thomas Law, Rev. H. Eivet Lewis Dr. Bendel Harris, and Gipsy Smith. It is likely that this will be only the commence- ment of a permanent feature of Free Church Council work, and that next" year,meetings will be held in m,ore than one centre, some town in the West probably being chosen in addition to Harrogate. , •

div.head: GIPSY SMITH.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH.

Gipsy Smith is preparing himself for his season's work, which this year includes an Autumn visit to the States. A Send-off meet- inp; is to be held in the middle of September at Liverpool, and a series of missions in America will commence in-October. Gipsy will probably re- turn to England in February. An Urgent request for his services has come from Atthtralia. It is hoped in the near future that arrangements may be made for him to visit the Commonwealth.

div.head: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.

During this hot and trying weather the thoughts of Wesleyan Methodists have been centred on the Wesleyan Conference at Not- tingham. The Rev. Albert Clayton is President. Mr. Clayton is known chiefly as the excellent Secretary of the Connexional Funds, and it is don tless his splendid service in connection with the Twentieth Century Fund that secured his elevation to the Presidency. Among the interesting, reports which will bp presented to the Conference is that of the lanchester and Salford Mission. The Mane ester Mission under the charge of Rev. S. F. Collier, is doing a wonderful work in that city. There are fifteen c entres for evangelistic and social service. It is impossible even to summarise the various agencies comprised in this wonderful work, for which the most abundant success is to be wished.

div.head: WORN IN THE VILLAGES.
div.p: WORN IN THE VILLAGES.

The National Free Church Council during the summer months runs a Mission Van for use in the rural districts. The Rev. Jese Mayo, who is in charge of this van, gives an interestin account of his tour in this mouth's Fre Church Chronicle. Mr. Mayog .s astonished at what he calls "the heathen darkness which may and does accompany ritualistic practices," and he finds in some of the smaller villages there is great need of light. The work which Mr. Mayo accomplishes should be of much service in this direction.
OUR PURITAN lIERITAGP..

More and more attention is 'being given to history, and it is always interesting th trace the influence of former times on the life of the pre- sent. Dr. John Brown, who is perhaps the greatest living authority on Puritan times, has written for this month's Free Churchman an article on "Our Heritage from the Indepen- dents." Dr. Brown shows in a clear and interesting way what we owe to our Independent forefathers. The article is well illustrated with pictured of Puritan divines, &c.

div.head: MALTA SCANDAL.
div.p: THE MALTA SCANDAL.

A .few weeks ago the Rev. John McNeill, the well-known Evangelist, conducted a mission among the Protestants of Malta. These meet- ings somehow raised the ire of the Roman Catholic Archbishop, who protested to the Governor against the services. A lengthy cor- respondence ensued in which the Archbishop claimed that the meetings ought to he discon- tinued as objectionable to the Roman Catholic population. Extraordinary as it may seem, although the Governor disputed the Arch- bishop's reasoning, he (the Governor) requested Mr. McNeill to t'discontinue. The matter was recently brought before the General Com- mittee of the National Free Church Council, which passed the following resolution :—" The Execntive Committee of the National Council of the Evangelical,. Free Churches emphatically protests against the, recent unwarrantable in- terference of the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Malta with the Rights of Citizenship under the British Flag. It.greatly regrets the suppression on the part of the Military Governor and his Britannic Majesty's High Commissioner, of peaceful religious services conducted in the Opera House by an eminent Minister of 'the United Free Church of Scotland (RL v. John McNeill) and at the dictation and demand of an alien prelate; and it calls upon his Majesty's Government to uphold the common privileges of civil and religious freedom which obtain everywhere throughout his Majesty's Dominions, and the rights and liberties of worship and of free speech which exist under the British flag." It is probable that a deputation will wait upon the officials at the Foreign Office from the National Council to protest against this extra- ordinary action.

div.head: cyg.ols,!ossip
div.p: cyg.ols,!ossip

Cycling in Scotland. ist returned from a visit to the Western High- s, the writer is more than ever impressed with beauties of Scotland as a touring ground. highest mountains, the deepest lochs, and the est scenery are all found in the west. For the b part the roads are admirably graded, though laces the surface is a little loose. Few motor are encountered, and the light showers make an unknown quantity. It often happens that miles the road follows the course of a river 7, or runs along the shores of •a loch, as, for Iple, at Loch Awe, Loch Tay, and Loch ond. div.head: Renaissance of the Tricycle.
div.p: The Renaissance of the Tricycle.

Quite a number of good rides have been performed this season on three-wheelers, and there is no doubt that the modern tricycle, fitted with light wheels and tyres, and moderately geared, is a wonderfully speedy machine onsgoocl roads. On the other hand, on inferior highways the necessity of finding three tracks instead of one is a drawback which the lug. gage-laden tourist would be quick to notice, while the space needed for storage and its slightly in- creased first cost are minor points against the

tricycle. The all-weather rider sets considerable store on the stability of the three-tracker, as com- pared with the liability of tho safety to side-slip. The latest startling achievement 18 the ride of Mr. E. Buckley, of the Anfield 8.C., on a tricycle with constrictor tyres, geared Co 67 in. Starting from near Knutsford, Mr. Buckley covered 100 miles in 6 hrs. 54 min., 1061 miles in 12 hrs., and 303 miles in 24 hrs. In the last two instances the pre- vious record was beaten by and 28 miles respec- tively. The Holiday Tour.

Holidays are the absorbing topic of the hour— narratives from those just returned, post cards from those away, and plans of those about to start. Nearly all the cabs and railway omnibuses, convey- ing passengers to the London termini, have their roofs piled with several bicycles, in addition to the inevitable bags and boxes. The anxiety to start and reach the proposed destination by the quickest means influences the great majority of holiday- makers in favour of the railway. In many cases, however, where the members of a party are all riders, much pleasure would be experienced by making the journey by road. Of course, the lug- gage could still be sent by rail, although it would have to be paid for unless accompanied hy a pas- senger. Even in the hottest weather a road journey, leisurely undertaken, is more pleasurable than the monotony of a railway carriage and, if divided into suitable stages, need not be unduly tiring. This is especially the case when a cross-ceuntry route is to be followed, involving, on a railway tedious waits at function stations. _

REMARKABLE HAMMOCK ACCIDENT. Alfred Young, of Walton-road, Birkdale, slung a hummock between two walls at the back of his house, and while lying in it both walls gave way. Young was buried in debris. He sustainad serious injuries, and had to be taken to the Southport Infirmary.

A fashionably dressed woman, named Alice Buck, described as a dressmaker, of Leeds, was sent to prison for six months at Harrogate on Tuesday for a long series of thefts from jewellers' shops in the town. It was stated that the woman came of a respectable family but had been addicted to laudanum taking.
