The Examiner, Saturday, August 4, 1906.

THE SEASIDE MAGAZINE. The" Strand Magazine " for August rightly bears al holiday look, and will be much prized by all those who are bound for the sea-shore. Sir A. Conan Doyle, the favourite of " Strand " readers, opens the ball with another long instalment of that splendid serial," Sir , Nigel," and the illustrations which accompany it are ' remarkable for their beauty of execution as well as for 1, the wonderful accuracy in historical detail. An interest- ing article is that which deals with the "Curiosities of a Razor Edge." The article discloses, by means of micrographs, some very unexpected facts about razors, and the way they do their work, and demonstrates without a doubt that the edge of a good razor is not really "sharp," and is very far from being smooth. " Two on an Island "is a pretty story by that delighful writer, C. C. Andrews, and "The Chronicles of the Strand Club "are as amusing as ever. " Pack of Pook's Hill," by Rudyard Kipling, discloses this author's remarkable talent in a new vein in this month's story, entitled "Hal o' the Draft." The Bishop of London is depicted at different ages in" Celebrities," his early portraits being most interesting." Humour by Post ' illustrates the remarkable rise of the picture post-card, and is illustrated chiefly from drawings by the date Phil May. 4 Living Figures " is a most ingenious article, in the course of which the author explains, by means of the most remarkable drawings we have ever seen, the ease with which statistics can be made attracting and highly interesting. " Alf's Dream," by W. W. Jacobs, is a most amusing naval yarn in the author's inimitable style, and is followed by " The Gaines of Animals," with life-like illustrations by C. Pearse. " Scenes of Famous Songs " gives interesting particulars of the birthplace of such famous songs as " Rock of Ages," "The Garden of Sleep," "John Peel," "On the Banks of Allan Water," "Annie Laurie," " Ye Banks and Braes o' Bonnie Doon," " Killarney,"" The Fair Maid of Wicklow," &c. Lady Henry Somerset contributes a capital story entitled" At the Crossing," and " Prince Fantasto " will delight the crowds of " Strand " children. The pages of" Curiosities "close what must be acknowledged by even the most fastidious reader as L a wonderful sixpennyworth.

div.head: OFFICE OF ALDERMAN.
div.p: THE OFFICE OF ALDERMAN.
MANCHESTER CITY COUNCIL'S REMARKABLE ACTION.
Petition for Election by Ratepayers.

The Manchester City Council on Wednesday, by a majority of two, passed a resolution that Parliament be petitioned to amend the Municipal Corporations Acts with respect to the office of aldermen, so as to provide for their being directly elected by the ratepayers In a leading article on the matter, the Manchester Evening Chronicle "is particularly outspoken. " Many a true word," says this journal, is spoken in je'st.' And many jests ware made on Wednesday at the expense of Manchester's Aldermen. The greatest joke of all was that a resolution asking for their election by the ratepayers was actually carried. Of course, it was in a thin house, after a perfunctory debate,and on what the high and mighty would describe as a snatch division. But that is one of the oddities of the Manchester City Councillors. They not infrequently take the right course by accident, and shrink abashed afterwards at their own temerity. In a fall Council and a full-dress deoate they are apt to be over-awed by their associa- tions. And most easily of all are they over-awed by their Aldermen. With what repentance will they realise to-day that, in a weak moment they have shown themselves so strong as to send up to Parliament a petition for the ending, or mending, of the system , under which the Aldermen are appointed ! It is significant that not even an Alderman lifted up his voice against the proposal, though with one or two exceptions they valiantly held up their bands against it. If the idea of unelective, unrepresentative persons sitting upon a public body is in general repugnant to modern ideas of self-government ; in Manchester, in particular, the anomaly has not an argument in its favour. . . . .

Here or there it may be contended that the power ot co-option gives the members of a Council an opportunity to strengthen their administrative ability by the selection of outsiders of special knowledge in, or aptitude for, particular branches of municipal work. Elsewhere it may be claimed, at least, that a dominant party can be strengthened by the addition of leaders who have failed at the poll or by the mere increase of voting strength in the Chamber. But the question of strengthening anything or anybody does not enter into the arrangement by which the Alderinanic ranks of the Manchester Council are recruited and retained. Here, by a system which has at least the merit of simplicity, there is one, and one only, qualification for Aldermanic promotion. It is seniority. In due course, if not at the moment of selection, it becomes senility. But what matter? Once an Alderman,always an Alderman. A system which requires no other qualification on appointment could not logically introduce a test after- wards. So once ensconced in his comfortable seat, a Manchester Alderman becomes a privileged person for the rest of his days. He cannot be called to account for his actions : he need not, indeed, have any actions to account for. Like Shakespeare's pantaloon, he may be content to continue, sans everything, till kindly Nature brings to himself and to the community a merciful release. The picture is not overdrawn, as anyone can say who knows the composition of the Aldermanic bench in this city and the manner in which men, once capable and competent, are content to linger on amid the growing infirmities of mind and body until they reach the stage when, as Lord Randolph Churchill once described it they possess all the attribute of extreme age—except wisdom. On the Manchester City Council there are thirty-one Aldermen. Of these, an intelligent observer could count—almost on the fingers of one hand, easily upon ' the fingers of both—the full list of those who are in any sense an assistance in the government of the city. And of these, there is not one whose zeal would not be quickened, and whose ability would not be better directed by being made, as other members are, respon- sible to the public in the management of whose affairs he is allowed to take a prominent part. How many people have noticed the extent to which. the Aldermen contrive to monopolise everything that is worth monopolising in connection with the Corporation ? In view of their quantity and quality it is a amazing how they are allowed to boss the show. On every important comrnitteethey enjoy a pre- ponderence as suggestive as it is surprising:. On the Parliamentary Sub-Committee, which has the inaugura- tion of all legislation in connection with the Corpora- tion, there are 22 Aldermen to n Councillors ; on the Noraihations Committee which settles the composition of every other committee they are eight to six. On the Waterworks Committee they are eleven to six. Of a committee of six yesterday appointed to select a new Lord Mayor four are Aldermen. Who would suppose that their total strength is only one-fourth of the Council ? Is there any good thing going, the Aldermen are mat it. The city has three representatives on the govern- ment of Victoria University. Three of them are Aldermen ! The Gamma appoints eleven Ship Canal Directors—an office with very special attractions. Ten are Aldermen! Where the common Councillors get a chance is on the committees where there is !tore work than .glory. On the Baths and Wash-houses Committee the Aldermen are modest enough to be content with one representa- tive among twenty. On the Parks and Cemeteries they I have four to fifteen Councillors,on the Paving Committee four to fourteen, and on the Cleaning three to sixteen! It is as well that the public should. know and notice these peculiarities in the distribution of power. What- ever the result of Wednesdays division,it is really time the matter was seriously taken in hand. Without wait- ing for Parliamentary legislation the Councillors, if they would take their courage in their hands, could promptly, with the help of the citizens, put a stop to some of the most glaring evils of the present system. The " Manchester Guardian" says : "The resolution adopted by the City Council to petition Parliament in favour of an alteration of the Municipal Corporations Act to make aldermen subject to popular election is of distinct interest. The survival of aldermen is directly due to the House of Lords. The famous Commission of 1835 reported in favour of a governing authority consisting only of directly elected members. The House of Lords opposed the whole scheme of reform, but under pressure from Sir Robert Peel consented to a compromise which retained a proportion of alderman. Since then, however, there has been a tendency in the direction of popular election. The Act of 1835 restricted the choice of corporations to their own members •, to-day they may elect any citizen. The abstract democratic theory of course demands direct election, but in England the indirect election of the national executive has been the accepted working rule. Aldermen cannot, however claim the privileges of Cabinet Ministers, for they are in no sense the muncipal executive, any more than are ordinary councillors. A fair theoretical case might be made out for them never- theless. There is a favourite of the political philosopher, the excellent and capable citizen eager to serve his fellows but unwilling to face the hurlyburly of an election. We are not sure that he is very numerous, but something might be said for a provision which admits him to the public service while sparing him the terrors of a con- test. The theory would make the title of alderman the highest distinction which a city could confer. Between the theory and the practice, however, there is, we fear, a great distance. How many corporations exercise their power to elect aldermen outside their own body? The custom is for the aldermanic chair to be the reward of seniority rather than of distinction—a reward which, by an unwritten law, confers lifelong office free from all responsibility to the public. Such a custom destroys I the theoretical argument for the indirect election of I aldermen, and indirect election cannot survive unless it justifies its existence by securing the services of a body of men who in talent and efficiency are really the most distinguished in the city.

div.head: MAGAZINE CUTTINGS.
div.p: MAGAZINE CUTTINGS.

THE MAN BEHIND THE GUN. An interesting point was mooted in our hearing not long since (writes " H. in "Country Life ") in reference to the hard-hitting and clean-killing power of rival guns and cartridges. The point was that these qualities may depend partly on the physical develop- raent of the man behind the gun, and on his own shoulder resistance to the weapon at the moment of its discharge. Without attempting to dogmatise on the matter, we are prepared to believe that there may be something in the point. One advocate of this view even went so far as to insist that the gunner might even, by a forward push of his shoulder, or deliberate extra muscular resistance, at the psychological moment, help his gun to make a longer and cleaner kill when necessity arose

MONSTER ART DRAWING. In the current issue of " Tit-Bits " full particulars are given of a Monster Art Drawing, in which prizes to the value of £l,lOO are offered, in addition to five thou- sand or more other prizes. This great art drawing, in which the prizes will be paintings selected by the winners from the Royal Academy, &c., will take place publicly in the presence of the managing committee approved by the Board of Trade, at the Queen's Hall, Langham Place, London, W., on November 21st, 190 G. This is a splendid opportunity to obtain a chance of procuring valuable pictures to beautify the home. In this week's issue, too, is made the announcement that yet another £lOO has been paid as an insurance claim, thus bringing the total amount paid by " Tit-Bits," in settlement of insurance claims, up to the grand total of

THE AUGUST "GRAND." The comfortable doctrine of the ineffable Dr. Pan- gloss that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds,is preached so usually that it is a positive relief to turn month by month to that very excellent epitome of fact and flu Lion, the" Grand Magazine," which dares to " tackle " all the burning questions of the day—great and small—from an independent point of view. An article that perhaps no existing periodical but the " Grand" would have dared to print, is that entitled, " How Bills are Taxed," which describes , the scandalous overcharges which even reputable firms of solicitors sometimes make when con- suited by confiding clients upon trivial matters. 1 As usual, too, the fiction, of which there appears to be a larger proportion than usual, is again super-excellent in character. There are stories to laugh at, stories to thrill us with horror, stories to evoke the tender tear of sympathy, and stories that, as our French neighbours say, give one furiously to think." Of the latter, the " League of Old Men," Jack London's " best story," is a most remarkable specimen. The new serial story, "The Botor Chaperon," which begins in this number, promises to excel, anything the popular authors, C. N. and A. M. Williamson, have yet written. Altogether the August" Grand "is another marvellous bargain for 4,1 d., even in an age of marvellous bargains. AN INCIDENT OF THE INVASION OF FRANCE. Order re-established, my uncle returned to the Maine, of which our house formed part. He found a Cossack carrying off our two last blankets, and a tussle took place between him and the soldier, one of whose comrades took my uncles part. Just as he was handing the blankets back, a pistol went off and the poor man ' fell dead. My uncle was arrested, marched into the middle of the square, and sentenced by a young officer in command to fifty strokes of the knout for having beaten a Cossack. My uncle declared that he had done no such thing: but the Cossack who had accused him swore it was true, that he recognised him by his overcoat, and had been kicked by him. My uncle again declared his innocence but without. effect. Then, turning to the young officer, he said You are very young, and in a strange ceuntry. It may be you will yet have need of my services.' The officer laughed at him, and ordered the sentence to be carried out.—Some time afterwards my uncle saved the life of this very man. I was present when in his turn he pleaded for mercy. My uncle, after showing him the marks of the knout, said, I will show you how a Frenchman avenges himself,' and he had the young man conveyed to a place of safety. He was loud in protestations of gratitude, but we never heard of him again.—From " At Montmirail in 1814." in the "Corn- hill Magazine" for August. A ROWING-MACHINE.

One of the famous athletes included in a set of twenty-two cartoons entitled " Sports and Games," reproduced from Vanity Fair in the original colours in the August "Windsor," is Mr. S. D. Muttlebury, of whom the chronicler says "Mr. S. D. Muttlebury, one of the broadest-backed and finest oarsmen that ever lived, had the driving power of a steam engine and the endurance of a drome- dary. As his biographer said of him in Vanity Fair : 'At Eton he developed into a rowing-machine,and in that capacity he has since worked with regularity, breaking down much less often than the machinery of any of her Majesty's ships has been known to break down in an equal space of time.' He revived rowing at Cambridge with such effect that that University won tour successive victories over Oxford, though they had previously been in a very bad way. His biographer, in his concluding remarks, was undoubtedly severe upon Muttle,' and it was wispered amongst oarsmen at the time : 'Lo !an enemy bath done this!' For though he was never a scholar, he was a good- tempered great-hearted young man; and though he was never a brilliant conversationalist, he was not without a sense of humour."—The August " Windsor Magazine" is a splendid Holiday Number, containin,, stories by Anthony Hope, S. R. Crockett, Jack Condon, P. G. Wodehouse, Frances Rivers and other favourite novelists, besides many valuable and entertaining articles. An appreciation of " The Art of Mr. Marcus Stone, R.A.," is accompanied by seventeen plates from his most successful pictures. "THE SMART SET."

In the August number of" The Smart Set "a host of entertaining stories will be found. The novelette, in particular, will prove interesting reading. It is called The Purple Border," and is written by Beatrix Demarest Lloyd, a young writer of rare promise. The story opens in Ireland, where Mich;cl Derevarah, the eccentric young hero, is preparing to leave for America, after relinquishing his claims to the title of an earl. , Upon his arrival in Newport, where he visits an old boyhood friend, the real story begins, and a story more pill of charm and fine sentiment has seldom appeared in any magazine. It will win many admiring readers. The short stories are varied and uniformly excellent. William Hamilton Osborne, in "The Writ of Habeas Corpus," has told with much skill a tale which reads like a chapter from real life. " When the girls came out to play," by Dorothea Deakin, is a bright, light comedy, just the thing for a summer day. "A Matter of Habit," by Ludwig Lewisohn, is a powerful study of a woman and an egotist of whom she became enamoured. Her final awakening to the man's selfishness is brought about in an unusual way: " The Final Hour," by Katharine Metcalf Roof, is the story of an actress whose material instinct has been warped, but is at length made whole and clean. ' Eunice," by Anna McClure Sholl, and "As told by Renaud's Wife," by Anne Warner, are excel- lent pieces of fiction ; and there are other con- tributions by Mary Glascock, J. Saukville Martin,Leila Burton Wells, Charles Battell Loomis, and W. Carey Wonderly. The essay, by Richard Duffy, is entitled " Bohemia, New York." With quiet humour, Mr. Duffy describes that enchanting land, Bohemia, but there is much thought behind his light jesting. Poems by Florence Wilkinson, Mabel Earle, Ernest McGaffey, J. J. Bell, and others complete a most dis- tinguished issue of this magazine. THE NEW ROUTE TO IRELAND.

The new steamship service between Fishguard, on 1 the Pembroke Coast, and Ros3lare, on the East Coast 1 of Ireland, will shortly be inaugurated; and thus, says ' ENGINEERING, there will be realised a scheme long spoken of, and now carried out by a board composed of members from the directorates of the Great Western Railway of England and the Great Southern Railway of Ireland, which jointly own what is known as the Fishguard and Rosslare Railways and Harbour Company. For this new service the company have not only built three high-speed turbine steamers, but have constructed new harbours. Rosslare, continues ENGINEERING, formerly had only a small pier, which was quite inadequate for the company's requirements, while the site at Fishguard was a mass of precipitous rocks, varying in height from 100 ft. to 200 ft. The harbour improvements were commenced a few years ago, and at Rosslare there is now a pier 1,500 ft. long, and at Fishguard a splendid harbour, the natural advantages of the site having been augmented by a massive breakwater, some 2.000 ft. long, for the efficient protection of the new quay. The construction of this breakwater was a big undertaking, and about 1,500,000 tons of material obtained from the blasting away of the rocks already mentioned, were used in its formation ; it is 300 ft. broad at foundation, 70ft. at the top, which is about 20ft. above high-water level ; a lighthouse has been erected at the outer end. The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland opened on Saturday the new Rosslare Harbour and Railway. The new route is the most direct between London and the South of Ireland, and by placing vessels on the service with a speed of 221 knots, in combination with fast non-stop trains on both sides of the channel, the run , between the metroplis and Queenstown will be shorter by three hours than the fastest journey on existing routes. The vessels are handsomely fitted and most completely equipped, and are sure to become immensely popular with travellers and tourists to the , south and south-west of Ireland; while the speed, com- bined with the complete absence of vibration, ought to I dispel the terrors of a cross-Channel voyage for those to whom the mere mention of sea means ma de mer. , The vessels St. David and St. Patrick—the two built by Messrs. John Brown and Co., Limited—are triple-screw turbine steamers. They are, indeed, miniature Atlantic liners. The trials of the steame.rs, was arranged so as to , fairly represent the usual conditions of service, and over a course equal to the distance from Fishguard to Rosslare about 54 knots. The St. David attained a speed of exactly 23 knots, the engines and boilers working satisfactorily. The sister vessel—St. Patrick carried out a similar trial with almost identical results, a speed of 231 knots having been obtained under very easy steaming conditions.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN FIRE BRIGADE.

At the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Urban I District Council, on Wednesday, the Fire Brigade Com- mittee recommended that four 25-yard lengths of hose- pipe, with couplings, and two ladders be purchased to , replace those burnt at the recent theatre fire. hr. Imison said the town and owners of property were much indebted to Widnes Corporation brigade for services rendered at that fire. The committee ought to acquaint themselves with the real deficiences of the town in appliances for extinguishing fires, and whatever the cost might be, submit estimates, and lay the respon- sibility of not making provision on the Council. Votes of thanks were accorded the Widnes Corporation, Castner-liellner, and Ship Canal brigades for services rendered at the fire.

div.head: POLLCE INSPECTOU'S RETIRENIENT.
div.p: POLLCE INSPECTOU'S RETIRENIENT.

Inspector Proud, Widnes, retired from active work under the Lancashire County Constabulary on Tuesday, after twenty-five years strenuous service in the police force, which followed many years of active life in the Army, he having served with the 80th Foot Regiment, also in the Malay peninsula, China, and South Africa, taking part in the Perak expedition and the Zulu campaign. He joined the Lancashire 'Constabulary at Preston, and was nine years at Old Swan, seven at Bootle, seven at Seafortla, completing his term of twenty-five years at Widnes. He enjoyed the utmost respect of the townspeople.—Sergeant Tongue' who has been stationed at Prescot during eleven years, has been promoted to fill the vacancy. DEATH OF A WIDNES COUNCILLOR.

Much regret was felt in Widnes on Saturday at the death of Councillor Torn Laws which occurred at his residence, the Grosvenor Hotel. The deceased was most popular and widely known, chiefly through his connection with sport. For the last twelve months he had been ailing, while for the past two months he had been confined tp bed. Mr. Torn Laws represented Waterloo Ward dn the Town Council for the past eight years, and he rendered conspicuous service to the town on the Health Committee, of which he was the chair- man. Sport of all kind had his patronage. In his younger days he was a prominent runner. He held the record for attendances at Council meetings for many years, and was so diligent that he only missed one meeting out of almost 300 in four years. Sympathy is expressed on all sides with the wife and five children whom he leaves behind. PROPOSED BRUNNER BATHS FOR RUNCORN. At the meeting of the Runcorn Urban District Coun- cil on Wednesday the Highway and Buildings Com- mittee submitted the oiler of the Right Hon. Sir John Brunner to spend a sum not exceeding £3OO in making a swimming bath in the cooling pond at the waterworks in accordance with the plan of Mr. Wilding. It was recommended that the thanks of the council be given to Sir John, and that be be informed that his offer would receive careful consideration. Mr. Taylor, in moving the acceptance of this minute, said the need of baths had long been felt but ways and means had always been an olastanle. Mr.lmison said he was behind nobody in his feeling of thanks to Sir John for his generosity but they ought to know who had ventured to submit plans and specifications to Sir John, without the knowledge of the council, of a scheme which had been practicaliy rejected by the Council because the water was filthy and greasy. He asked them to consider whether they would not submit to Sir John a more permanent scheme, and ask him—he would not care to do it—to accept it and increase his contribution.—The minute was carried. PRESENTATION TO DEAN CLARKE.

There was a large lathering in the Girls' Schoolroom Newtown, Widnes, o the occasion of a presentation to Dean Cl Lrke upon his preferment to the Deanery of Appleton from St. Marie's, Newtown. Amongst those present were the Mayor (Alderman S. Quinn) in the chair, Dean Clarke, Fathers Quirk, Ryan, Rimmer (old curates), Western, Morrisey, Dooley, and Councillors P. Caldwell and F.Tallon. After a musical programme, the Mayor asked Councillor Talton to make the presentation of an illuminated address, beautifully inscribed, and Father Quirk to present the dean with a cheque for £1.30. Eulogistic speeches were made by the Rev. Fathers, the Mayor, and Councillor Tallon,who all testified to the dean's splendid qualities. For thirty- three years he had laboured in Widnes, and during his time devoted much attention to the subject of educa- tion. He had seen splendid progress made in the town. —The Doan,in acknowledging the gifts, said that his very heart and sohl were centred in the welfare of Widnes, and he hoped that he would be spared many years to labour amongst its inhabitants. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.

- - At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Messrs. F. J. Norman (in the chair), S. Taylor, T. D. Timmis, James Pritchard, and D. Bisbrown, Griffith Roberts, Warrington, was charged with having been drunk on the licensed premises of the Queen's Hotel on Sunday evening, and also with having assaulted P.C. Wareing while in the execution of his duty. He pleaded not guilty to both charges. P.C. Wareing said he was in Church-street at nine o'clock on Sunday evening and saw defendant and two other men. They were drunk. They went into the Man at the Wheel public-house and he followed them and turned them out. They went up Waterloo-road and into the Queen's Hotel. He followed and put defendant out. The other two men came out. When outside defendant struck him. He fought defen- dant and one of the other men for about five minutes, when defendant's companion got clear away. He called on a man named Wakefield to assist him. While he was struggling with prisoner the third man struck him on the nose and felled him to the ground. James Brookes, licensee of the Queen's Hotel, said the defendant and the other two came into the hotel at half-past nine. They were very drunk, and were refused, and told to go out, The officer came in and removed defendant. The others went. He saw the men violently assault the officer. Defendant who denied the offences was fined ss. for the first case and for the second Ns. and costs, £2 is. 6d., or a month's imprison- ment,

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
RAILWAY SERVANI'S' CHURCH' PAR WE.

The different sections of railway servants at St. Helens and St. Helens Junction combined on Sunday to hold their second annual church parade at Si. Helens Parish Church for the benefit of the Railway gon's Convalescent Homes and other benevolent institutions. The bulk of the railway men present were in uniform, and the attendance included Ar. R. Whistlocroft,station master, St. Helens •, Ar. J. Lucas, St. Helens Junction ; Inspect& Bonney, Ar. W. Aiddlehurst, and Hr. Evans. The Sutton-road Prize Band headed the procession and accompanied the singing in church. Ar. Whistlecroft read the lesson.and. the Rey. Cyril. Budsley (vicar) gave a stirring address. WATER POLO. St. Helens and Lancaster met on Saturday night in the St. Eielens Cerperation B Wks in the second round for the Lancashire Cup. Beth teams were at full strength. St. Helens attacked strongly, evidently determined to avene the crushiag. defeat they sus- tained the Tuesday previous. They could not however, penetrate the visitors' defence for some time, and scrappy play was the order. Later, Lancaster asserted themselves, and won by 4 goal 3 to 3. Humphreys and Armistead scored one each, and Duke scored two for Lancaster. Lomax scored all three for St. Helens.

SCHOLARSHIP RESULTS. The result of the examinations for scholarships under the St. Helens Education Committee's scheme has just become known. Five scholarships for boys were offered, and these have all been won by twelve-year- old boys from Cawley Council Schools, the successful scholars being Joseph S. Williams, Thomas Jackson, H. C. Howell, Wallace M.. Inman, and C. B. Bamford. In the girls' section, the following six head the list : —NI. Bradshaw, Windle School ; NI. E. Jones, Raven- head ; Ethel Welsby, Rayenhead ; E. Slater, Cowley Council ; A. sigeatherell, St. Mary's and El. tkl. Patterson, Windle. For the pupil teachers' scholarships, Robina Bickerstaffe,of Cowley Council, heads the list with 332 marks, and the other' successful candidates are Ada Ingram, Nellie Kenyon, Ernest Gough, May Elesford, Ellen Halsall, Edgar Lea, John Naylor,J. A. O. Chadwick, Edward Doolau, Violet Nlyerscoug'a, May Saggerson, John J. Turton,S lmund B ardsley, Nlarie Batt en,Nlargaret Byce, Margaret Nicholas, Annie Masker, Sydney W. Dennett, and Maggie Lacey. . TECHNICAL SPLTDENI'S' SUCCESS. ' . _

The authorities at the Municipil Tahnicll Schools at the Gamble Institute, St. Elelens, have received intima- tion that two of the students have attained the highest hononrs in the country in mechanical engineering and machine drawing. Mr. J; W. E. G. Wright ha 4 been awarded the silver nwlal of the City and Guilds of Loudon Institute,and :Mr. W. E. Taylor has been awarded the bronze medal, these being the highest; awards in the kingdom. Mr. Taylor, who is only eighteen, has also won the silver modal in connection with the same work awarded by the Board of E lunation, South Kensington. These notable successes have given the greatest satis- faction throughout all the departments of the Technical Schools. PLUCKY CONSTABLE REWARDED.

- - The St. Helens Watch Committee have complimented Police-constable Foster, of the borough force, for his plucky conduct in trying to rescue a boy wha had sunk in the canal near Cannington ani Shaw's works a few weeks ago, and they have granted him a reward of .C 3 and instructed the Chief Constable to bring the matter before the notice of the Royal Humane Society. NEW SCHOOLS.

The St. Helens Education Committee have decided to proceed with the building of the new Cowley Council Elementary School,and the architect has been instrncted to complete the plans. Tenders have been accepted for the Cambridge-road cookery centre, which is to be built by Mr. Fred Brown. The Board of Education have unofficially approved the draft plans for the alteration at the Cowley Grammar Schools, and also of certain alterations in the structure of the new schools to be built at Parr. For the latter school .£18,509 is to be borrowed, and £3,600 for the alterations to Cowie schools.

div.head: ST. HELENS SCHOLARSHIPS AWARDED.
div.p: ST. HELENS SCHOLARSHIPS AWARDED.

The St. Helens Education Committee, after consider- ing the report on the recent scholarship examinations, have awarded scholarships as follows :—Unconditional scholarships to Cowley Middle Schools: Joseph S. Williams, T. Jackson, H. C. Howell, W. M. Inman, C. B. Bamford, Polly Bradshaw, Mary E. Jones, Ethel Welsby, Evelyn Slater, Ada Weatherell, and H. M. Patterson. Pupil teacher scholarships: Robina. div.head: ST. HELENS DX;TOR'S ACTION.
div.p: A ST. HELENS DX;TOR'S ACTION.

On Wednesday in the Chancery Court of Lancashire, Vice-Chancellor Leigh Clare, sitting at St. George's Hall, resumed the hearing of the action in which Dr. E. T. Twyford, of Ormskirk-street, St. Helens, sought an injunction to restrain the Argentina Meat Company, Limited, from continuing an alleged nuisance. The defendants have installed refrigerating plant in a butcher's shop next door to Dr. Twyford, and he com- plains of the noise which it creates and the inconveni- ence so occasioned. Farther evidence as to the alleged nuisance was heard. For the defence Mr. Maberley contended that the refrigerating plant set up no nuisance. If it made any noise at all it was only such , as the circumstances of the neighbourhood and exigencies of the business justified. A number of witnesses were called, one of them stating that the plant was erected on a concrete bed, which deadened the noise and vibra- tion. His Honour arranged to visit the premises and plant. On Tuesday next, he said, he would be in a position to make a statement to counsel regarding his conclusions, and then he would hear their arguments as to those conclusions.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
HAYDOMC COAL STEALERS.

At Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday, Ann Bellls, charged with stealing coal from a dirt heap at Elaydock, preaded "guilty of picking it up."—P.C. Williams deposed to finding her with her son, taking the coal, on the afternoon of July lfith.—Mr. Addison proved having shown her a printed notice against taking the coal.— Pined 10s. including costs.—:ll.lry Owen Jones, who was summoned for lvst Bench day, but did not appear, admitted a similar offence.—P.C. Williams said that when he caught her in the act alonn, with another woman who was fined at the last Court, the woman gave a wrong address.—Fined 10s., including costs.

WEDDINGS AT EARLESTOWN. A wedding of local interest was solemnised at St. John's Church, Earlestown last Thursday, in the presence of a large congregation. The choir attended and the organist played suitable music before and after the ceremony, whilst the Vicar officiated. The bride- groom was Mr. Samuel Tucker, of Lawrence-street, a member of the Vulcan Foundry office staff, and the bride Miss E. A. Carter, of Clarence-street, for smne years a teacher at the District School. She wore a grey dress faced with gold aol white, with hat to match. Her two sisters were bridesmaids,dressed in blue with black hats. She was given away by her brother. and Mr. Jos. Taylor Edington officiated as groomsman. The honeymoon is being spent at Matlock. Among the presents were a silver cruet and a silver jam dish from' the staff of the District School and other presents from individual members of the teaching profession in the district.—At the Wesleyan Church on the same day Mr. Peter Ashton of Buttonwood, a member of the staff of Bold Colliery, was married to Miss Ann Southern, of Nelson-street, Earlestown. The Rev. F. R. Smith officiated. DAMAGE TO CROPS.

John Griffin was summoned at Newton before Messrs. Gillespie and Robinson last Thursday for damaging a growing crop of turnips belonging to Samuel Kirkham. —Mr. E. A. White, prosecuting, said the complainant suffered great loss by raids on his farm (Lawson's Farm, Newton). Peas and ether growing crops were continually being taken. On a recent Sunday night the plaintiff and his son watched in a turnip field till about ten o'clock, when the father went indoors, leaving the son still on the out-look. About half-past ten Mr.

_ Kirkham, jun., heard people coming along the cindered lane from the Bottle Works Ashton-road. He heard them planning for some of them to go round by Ashton- road to ',,et some peas, while others watched. One man was left at the stile, and looking down the hedge he saw Kirkham there. Kirkham said "I've copped you this time," and then several of them went up to him— including this defendant—and threatened to "knock his neck out." The two Kirkhams took Griffin to the police station, where he said " You have insulted my wife." What Possible suggestion there cr_nld be in that, he (irr. White) could not say. Air. Kirkham did not know Origin or his wife, and there had been no woman present at all. The damage done to the young turnips by being trodden down was put at the nominal charge of Is. Or course there was great difficulty in assessing the damage done by any one ?f the °fie Iders.—Samuel Kirkham, son or the complainant, gave vidence bearing out Mr. White's statement.— Defendant pleaded guilty to the charge, but said that when he was going round the Oak Tree corner earlier in the evening -with his wife, stories were throwa at them over the hedge. He went home and took his coat off, and then went to see if he could find out who they were that threw the stones.—The Bench could not see that that accounted for what Sir. Kirkham had spoken of, and they ordered defendant to pay the costs and is. damage, and h tlf a guinea for the advocate's fee. VIADUCT INSTITUTE EXAMINATION RESULTS. div.head: NEWTON CONSERVATIVES. Quarterly Council Meeting. COL. PILKIN—GITON— AND THE ARMY SCHEME.
div.p: NEWTON CONSERVATIVES. Quarterly Council Meeting. COL. PILKIN—GITON— AND THE ARMY SCHEME.

The quarterly meeting of the Council of the Newton Division Conservative Association was held on Satur- day afternoon at the Central Offices, Newton-le- Willows. Mr. C. B. F. Borron presided, and among those present were Colonel R. Pilkington, C. 8., Mr. W. Collingwood, Mr. W. Holland-Owen, Mr. P. Mather, &c. Lord Newton wrote regretting his inability to attend. During the course of a brief address, Colonel PHking- ton, referring to the Government's proposals with regard to the army, said Earl Roberts, who was admit- tedly one of our greatest military authorities, had stated that the array as it now stood was not sufficient to do the ordinary police work of the nation. In spite of this opinion Mr. Haldane wag determined to cut down the strength of the infantry by 20,000 !men. In other words, he would destroy the best organization of the army, and limit the reserves. It was a terrible mis- take. On every one of the professional soldiers who had been in training for ,two years an average of .£2OO had been spent. If these proposals were carried out, it meant the destruction of four millions' worth of regular soldiers ; and it would mean also the removal of at least 20,000 men into the ranks of the unemployed. Earl Roberts condemned the scheme right and left. He was alarmed, and undoubtedly if these ideas assumed practical shape they would strike a tremendous blow at the force. The whole scheme was a piece of reckless machiess from beginning to end and the same unsound policy had been practised in regard to the Navy. Con- cluding, Colonel Pilkington made reference to the Education Bill. In his opinion it had not been improved in any particular. It was as unsatisfactory as when it was first framed, and from beginning to end was an unjust and tyrannical measure, framed for the gratification of an extreme section of the Government's supporters. (Applause.)

Walter Skudder has completed ten years' attendance at Vicarage-road School, Plumstead, without being once late or absent. Daniel Edwards, a collier, was killed at Duffryn Colliery, Aberdare, on Wednesday night. He fell from a cage, suspended a few yards from the surface, to the bottto.n of the shaft.

R. dePrez, Lower Walton, which at present is in full bloom, for the first time for trl,*en.ty years. This curious plant is a "Yucca "rlartosa.'" and is a native of the West Indies. The people of Pendleton are also glorying in the ,possession of a "Yucca Gloriosa " in their park, the 'lower of which however, is hardly to ~be compared with that owned by Mr. de Prez. * 5 * About six months ago the Stockton Heath Parochial C ommittee embarked upon the task of revising the local bye laws on the lines of the model bye-laws drawn up by the Local Grovernrnent Board. When the sub-committee has corn- Veted its deliberations, whatever criticism may be „urled at its head, it cannot be charged with undue 4aste. * * * "The Clewer St. Stephen Parish Magazine " c_announcing that the Sunday school will have to be "vliz r a short time while the building is being hope repaired extends the following admonition: We do that a held the pwreti the Church Sunday school is not 8 will not send the children to No n- conformist schools It is better to stay at home, or go to some sery the Lord's Da iee, or otherwise profitably employ ceivably mean 7.st: Profitably employ," might con- 1 breaking the No sling the Nonconformist purse, ' . aconformist window, or outraging . the Nonconformist conscience in the estimation of the good Christian who Penned the heartfelt appeal. 1 A. particularly mean theft from the" Lion" Hotelis ] reported this week.
